=== Case ===
CaseNumber: 01111943
Reported software version: Voalte Nurse Call 4.0.405
case_summary.summary: At Holy Cross Health, a code blue call in 3 South, CVIMC, Room 360 did not annunciate at the primary location. Investigation found the GRS10 serving the PBX station was repeatedly going into recovery mode, and after shared-RCB wiring was investigated and the GRS10 at the PBX was eventually replaced, the customer confirmed functionality; a Chronos report confirmed the code blue call did alert for the room, though the PBX did not see the call because the device was in recovery mode at the time.
case_summary.reported_issue: Code blue call did not annunciate at the primary staff console for the room.
case_summary.product: GRS10 / PBX station, Nurse Call system
case_summary.actions_taken: Checked that the call device, dome light, and staff console operated normally during testing.
Found no system alert present at the GRS10 during the time of the incident.
Identified that the RCB for the PBX station was shared with another location, which may have caused rebooting.
Monitored the PBX station, which did not time out during observation; ping and interface checks showed no obvious faults.
Replaced the GRS10 at the PBX, pushed software, and updated configuration in ECT.
Customer tested and confirmed functionality.
case_summary.resolution: Replacing the GRS10 resolved the issue; a Chronos report confirmed the code blue call did alert for this room.
case_summary.status: resolved
case_summary.key_points: Root cause: GRS10 at the PBX repeatedly going into recovery mode.
RA_Test_Results__c states the GRS10 at the PBX continued to go into recovery mode, which conflicts with the case resolution stating replacement resolved the issue; the case resolution and actions-to-resolve fields were preferred here.
RA_Did_same_issue_occur__c: No.
HRCSVC_Injury_or_Death__c was asked but not provided, flagging it as a safety-relevant case.

root_cause_summary: The investigation determined that Room 360 successfully generated the Code Blue call locally, and the room's relay outputs activated as expected, confirming the initiating device functioned properly. However, the call was not annunciated at the expected consoles because the communication path between the room, primary console, and PBX infrastructure was disrupted at the time of the event.

Logs showed that shortly before the incident, the 3 South primary console experienced heartbeat and handshake failures to its rooted-device communication path. At the same time, GatewayService recorded socket communication errors involving the PBX GRS10 (10.244.57.65), indicating loss of connectivity within the alert distribution path.

Further analysis of the PBX GRS10 syslog identified a known software defect related to oversized message handling. GatewayService transmitted oversized packets that triggered packet framing/deserialization failures on the PBX GRS10, causing application faults and watchdog-triggered reboots. This behavior is consistent with known defect https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-20964#icft=NC-20964. The resulting PBX GRS10 failure placed the device into recovery mode and prevented it from receiving or processing Code Blue events during the incident window

troubleshooting_results: replacing GRS10 resolved issue, Chronos report confirms that code blue call did alert for this room. However PBX did not see the call due to being in recovery mode
rca_review_comments: The Code Blue event originated correctly from Room 360 and activated local room indicators; however, a failure in the upstream communication path prevented the alert from being properly delivered to and processed by the console infrastructure. Investigation found that the PBX GRS10 experienced a software-related failure caused by oversized GatewayService messages, resulting in application faults and device reboots consistent with known defect NC-20964. Concurrent communication failures between the PBX path and primary console disrupted Code Blue annunciation, preventing the alert from being received at the expected monitoring locations

summary: ER Code Blue Call Failed to Alert at the PBX
description: * During a conference call Annette stated that a nurse accidentally set off a code blue. They heard the call in the ER but they never heard the call at the switchboard.  This event occurred at 1:55 am on 4/14/17 and was reported to Annette by the PBX Manager.
* Hill-Rom IE, Andy McNeese stated that the PBX did not have code blue set, but oddly enough it was for the Security PBX, he configured the PBX to monitor Code Blue calls to resolve the issue.
root_cause_summary: Inconclusive; The secondary console monitoring criteria settings in the database does not log historical changes.
investigation_details: * Root Cause is inconclusive: The secondary console monitoring criteria settings in the database does not log historical changes. I reviewed all available database backups on the server and found that the PBX CCD was not configured to monitor the code blue call type on 4/14/2017, I am not able to determine when this value changed or if the PBX CCD was ever configured to monitor the code blue call type due to a lack of database backups. 

* I reviewed the configuration from 4/14/2017, the “PBX CCD” with serial number 051150XZWIS was not configured to monitor the Code Blue call type. The “PBX CCD” with serial number 051150XZWIS on 4/14/2017 was configured to monitor the entire 1 South, and 1 West Nursing Units at Tristar Horizon Medical Center for the following call types only: 

Code 4, Code 99, Code Adam, Code Amber, Code Pink, Code White, Smoke Alarm Call, Duress Alert, and Rapid Response.

* I reviewed all available database backups on the server. And the PBX GRS10 was not configured to monitor the code blue call until 4/17/2017. The database available database backups go back to the 14th and because they do not show the value being changed.
verification_summary: RCA-196 has been reviewed by QA/RA.  The root cause was inconclusive due to the secondary console monitoring criteria settings in the database not logging historical changes.  Due to the lack of database backups, R&D was unable to determine if the PBX CCD was ever configured to monitor the code blue call type, and if so, when this configuration was changed.  Several corrective actions already exist to improve logging capabilities; these have been linked to this RCA.  No other corrective actions were identified by the RCA Team at this time.  RCA-196 can be moved to a state of Done.
rca_review_comments: Existing CA's linked

summary: GRS10 high CPU and reboots often
description: Primary console down after rebooting on own.  Seems errors with 10.190.12.128, 10.90.13.0, 10.190.13.128 logs

 GRS10 98%

 console with issue, 10.190.13.253

 audio delay to rooms greater than 15 seconds up to about 40 seconds.
root_cause_summary: (1) Initial incident, 9/24/2019: two GRS5s were stuck in recovery mode. Their RCB3s generated alerts in rapid succession and sent them through the RCB3 NUC (10.190.12.156) to the GRS10 primary console (10.190.13.253), pushing CPU on the NUC and GRS10 to about 98%, causing console reboots and 15-40 second audio delays to rooms. Replacing the two GRS5s stabilized the site. (2) Recurrences on 9/28, 10/3 and 10/8 (roughly every 5 days): the NUC logged TCP write failures and deserialization errors on corrupt or partial packets, then lost RCBs, the lost primary console and repeated reboots of the 3CX PBX (10.4.204.128), until the NUC was rebooted. Engineering attributed this to the customer network (customer-owned switches with known power problems; DHCP lease behavior suspected), but it wasn't confirmed.
investigation_details: Amilcar Ubiera and Steve Moore found the two recovery-mode GRS5s flooding alerts. Disabling those rooms and replacing the GRS5s ended the spike, and the bad units were shipped back (FedEx 113944138643 / 113944138654). For the recurrences, Steve Martin captured NUC logs; Steve Moore found socket write failures and packet deserialization errors on the NUC, which points to a network problem. Open questions to the customer were never answered: confirm the NUC and 3CX server MAC addresses differ, DHCP lease renewal frequency and server type, DHCP logs matching the event times, and antivirus exclusions.
rca_review_comments: Initial cause: failed GRS5 audio stations in recovery mode caused an alert storm; corrected by replacing them. Recurrences: probable customer network or infrastructure problem, not confirmed because the customer's information was never received. Workaround: reboot the RCB3 NUC. Follow-up items: find out why the returned GRS5s couldn't leave recovery mode, and why an RCB3 sends alerts in rapid succession when its audio station malfunctions; neither has a recorded result or defect.

summary: SRS Code blue did not alert
description: # 1st Fl, ER, Trauma Room - Code Blue Call Did not Announce
root_cause_summary: Root cause is blown diode D2_PWR which is a known issue for this SRS model/revision. This issue has been resolved in subsequent models and revisions (reference CRCO# C134673).
investigation_details: **HW Investigation**

Device arrived dead. Would not power up because +5V rail was shorted to Ground. Root cause is a blown diode D2_PWR, which is the catch diode for the 5V buck converter. For the P2594NNC1B11 with PCB BOM Agile PN: 164760 Rev 2, the D2_PWR component is a 60V part (MPN: LT1766EFE#TRPBF, Mfr: Linear Technology). Rev 3 of the PCB BOM contains the replacement parts which are rated at 100V – so the issue with this component was fixed by 2015/2016 model year and subsequent models (reference CRCO# C134673).

I found one similar case with this same version of the SRS (P2594NNC1B11):

* SN: 481309JWIS, NCMR0396716, Case: 23988 -- received/tested 14 June 2022
* Troubleshooting notes: “SRS is dead, no +5V. Catch diode, D2_PWR, short.  Known issue with this diode which has been corrected with alternate diode.”

Also worth noting is that the nurse station did receive a Lost Primary Audio Station Alert for ED1 and it was showing on the console prior to the Code Blue, see case in Salesforce. Therefore, the device was not functioning properly prior to the Code Blue event. Furthermore, the customer said they thought they had a pending ticket on their end to replace the device.

The site also had another SRS the month before that they asked for a replacement, serial number indicated it was the same week/year as the device for this case (04414089WIS). They rebooted the associated RCB device and the lost primary audio station alert was still present. Services team reached out multiple times to see if the replacement that was sent was installed and configured successfully for ED4 but received no response from the customer so that case (01040763) was eventually closed.

I replaced the D2_PWR with a working component and the device now passes FCT. Note that logs say partial fail because the VPD read/write test was skipped and the handset off hook test initially failed because I did not remove the handset from the FCT cradle in time and had to re-run the test – which passed on the second attempt.

description: Customer details:

Acct # 605080

Acct name:Lubbock County Hospital District



Issue- PBX console (Secondary GRS10) was showing 30 lost unit server alerts. Unable to receive Code blue alerts. Checking performance of the GRS10 it remains at a constant 98/99% for CPU usage for NNC. 

Cause- The CPU usage is due to the GRS10 failing to make connections to other NNC devices over port 50005. Most of the connections show a TIME_WAIT instead of ESTABLISHED. Further probing revealed these connection failures was due to a disabled GRS10H NUC on the same subnet as our effected GRS10. 

Resolution: Rebooting the disabled GRS10H NUC resolved the issue of the failed connections on our effected GRS10. After the reboot connections were established and NNC CPU utilization on the GRS10 went down. 

Reason for RCA- We need to confirm why a disabled NUC would cause this sort of issue.
comment_summary: A basement PBX console reported Lost Unit Server alerts, together with high NNC CPU utilization on a GRS10 even though the bed plugins were not in use. Removing all plugins except calls and repeatedly rebooting the GRS10H NUC cut the alerts from 30 to 17 and finally cleared them, although the plugin-related spiking was supposed to have been resolved after 3.9.401. Later work found Lost Unit Server and lost secondary console alerts persisting for a nursing unit that was disabled in ECT, and the alerts cleared only after removing that disabled unit from the secondary unit monitoring of the other primary console and of the PBX. In the final session, re-enabling monitoring and rebooting the PBX no longer reproduced the alerts, and the engineer disabled SNTP on a POE switch (firmware 1.0.23) that had been rebooted, then left the site monitoring for recurrence.

=== Case ===
CaseNumber: 01138390
Reported software version: Voalte Nurse Call 4.0.403
case_summary.summary: At Scotland Memorial Hospital, a code call in 2nd Floor Med Surg Room 202 was not alerting the primary station, with no alerts or errors seen on initial console review. The GRS5 was suspected as failing and was replaced with a GRS7, but unconfigured and lost-audio-station alerts persisted after the first replacement; a second GRS7 and an upgraded RCB3 (in place of the RCB2) were ultimately installed, after which related system alerts cleared and test calls opened audio channels successfully.
case_summary.reported_issue: Code call not alerting the primary station for a room, with the room's GRS5 code blue lever suspected of failing.
case_summary.product: GRS5/GRS7 and RCB, Nurse Call system
case_summary.actions_taken: VNC'd into the console and found no alerts or errors for the room.
Had the FST replace the GRS5 with a GRS7, pushing software and configuring the device.
Found alerts did not clear after the first GRS7 was installed; installed a second GRS7, performed a global push in ECT, and power-cycled the RCB, after which alerts returned.
Identified that the room's port needed an RCB3 to properly support the GRS7 and paged this out.
Replaced the existing RCB with a new RCB3 and the GRS7 with another new unit, then reconfigured in ECT.
case_summary.resolution: The GRS5 was replaced with a GRS7, and the RCB2 was replaced with an RCB3.
case_summary.status: resolved
case_summary.key_points: Root cause: wrong RCB board type installed; an RCB3 was needed to support the GRS7.
RA_Did_same_issue_occur__c: No.
RA_Test_Results__c and HRCSVC_Test_Results__c describe Lost Audio Station/Unconfigured alerts and a failed code blue test after the first GRS7 install, which reflects an earlier troubleshooting step rather than the final outcome; the final service note confirms alerts cleared and test calls succeeded after the RCB3 and second GRS7 were installed.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
I made the change to make this work.  But I would add that this code has never worked this way at least in the 3.x and 4.x time frame.  I had previously made this change in 4.2.000 for the rcb3 to work in this manner.  
The way it has worked previously is that a device is searched for after startup of the rcb.  And once a device has been recognized a lost device alert is created.  And regardless of what is done after this point the alert is there.    
That being said.  The alert will now be canceled if the device has removed.  And the rcb will resume looking for any audio station plugged into the port.  The most likely differences in behavior would be around what happens in the transition to configured or possibly config push.  But I didn't see anything in testing.  
Impact Assessment:  
NCP - Device Maintenance - Trivial  
Platform Impact:  
rcb/rcb2  
Product Labeling Impact:  
N/A  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  10/DEC/2025  
Attendees - Curtis Jones (Quality Engineering), Stephen Moore (Development Engineering)  
Minutes - I pulled in the initial test that failed to this defect, as well as created a new objective for the updated way we're handling the unconfigured device alerts. This is a trivial impact, but there are still two regression tests because the updates to the data table for the direct test P1575-TEST-3740 also required minor updates to the regression tests. Both parties agree to the testing effort.

description: NOTES from troubleshooting:

Logged into ENT server  
Primary: 10.6.220.142 >

Lost and unconfigured AS alerts for the following rooms

S3041 > Lost and unconfigured AS  
S3042 > Lost and unconfigured AS

S3058 >Lost and unconfigured AS  
Clean holding >Lost and unconfigured AS  
Pyxis > Lost AS (this was pre upgrade)  
Also other rooms such as consult and show lost primary AS

S3041, S3042 S3043 S3057 ,S3058  
All these rooms had RCB1 devices that were changed to RCB 3  
All RCBs are up and running  
only issue is with GRS5 devices

Service Portal  
Ran check on GRS5 devices  
Software is up to date  
IP's match what is shown in ECT (for the RCBs)

Attempted to push software  
Download failed: unable to reach device

Checked Software of RCB3 for unit  
None of the listed rooms above had the proper firmware applied (only downloaded)  
Applied 3.9.4 firmware  
All applied successfully

Checked back with primary console

S3041 > cleared  
S3057 > cleared

S3041, S3042, S3043, S3058 > remain

Ran global push > no change > shows affected devices to fail

Removed RCB config for RM 58 (10.6.220.83) Reboot  
No change

Removed GRS5 from ECT > ran config  
Reboot RCB 10.6.220.83

Removed device in ECT > saved

Added GRS5 back (device is discoverable)  
No change

Customer was in RM 58 and stated he had a spare  
Plugged spare in  
Configured in ECT  
Service portal  
Unable to download to device (device not showing a mac or ip)  
Shows database error  
Device does show updated in the database

Checked DB for device  
Shows assigned to room 58  
Shows only the serial number and room (no mac or IP)  
put old device back in  040140ZPWIS > configured 

Spoke to Ron Miller (he had a very similar issue today)  
He advised to replace the RCB3 with another

Customer replaced board 0102312EWM2  
Successfully changed device in ECT  
Downloaded and applied software in SP  
Device came up with new IP 10.6.220.94  
GRS5 in port 1 has new IP  
However GRS5 in port 2 still shows 10.6.220.83 (both in SP and the Database)

Ran global push > no change  
Reboot RCB no change



we cannot get the GRS5’s on port 2 to work for a few rooms, These are using RCB3's  
We have tried different RCB3's from completely different batches (issue persists)  
Different GRS5 > Issue persists  
When we revert to a RCB1  
The GRS5's work perfect

Kevin has replaced other rooms with RCB3's and both GRS5s work  
This issue is only ha
comment_summary: GRS5 devices connected to RS2 (port 2) of RCB3 units were not receiving configuration, while GRS5s on RS1 worked correctly; only 4 of 13 changed rooms failed, new RCBs from different batches did not help, and substituting RCB1s cleared the problem immediately. Diagnostics included a Wireshark capture during a failed software download to the port 2 GRS5 (download failed with connection lost), plus hillrom-version, ip addr and nncdiag device-configuration list output from the RCB3. The thread concludes that the device firmware version in use has a bug, fixed in Nurse Call 4.0, in the script that starts the PPP daemon for port two of an RCB3: it configures the PPP connection with up to three DNS servers when the RCB3's DHCP lease supplies three, but PPP only allows two, so the child GRS5 on port 2 gets no DNS resolution. Because DNS is used to resolve the Nurse Call server IP for device registration, the port 2 GRS5 cannot obtain configuration or software updates.

root_cause_summary: Customer-site network/PoE port issue affecting device connectivity and operation. When tested on bench was not able to reproduce the issue. No hardware fault identified.
investigation_details: Customer initially reported that the GRS10H was unable to establish audio and displayed the error message “Temporary problem placing call please try again later.” The customer replaced the device locally in an attempt to resolve the issue. During the on-site follow-up, the replacement device was then found to be unable to obtain an IP address. Once the port issue was addressed on the customer side, the replacement device was able to obtain network connectivity, be configured, and operate successfully. The original returned device was later evaluated in R&D and no fault was reproduced. The unit configured normally and was able to place and receive calls on the bench.
troubleshooting_steps: FCT Logs Attached in the comments. FCT passed for all the hardware tests on this device.

R&D Investigation:

* Reviewed the reported issue on primary GRS10 at 10.23.186.207 after the customer observed the message “Temporary problem placing call, please try again later” when answering calls.
* Confirmed the customer had already verified all RCB ports and did not identify any port-level fault.
* Checked the GRS10 for active alarms, alerts, or other visible fault indications at the time of investigation.
* Attempted to validate the issue condition, but the behavior was not reproducible during review.
* Bench-tested the returned original device in R&D by configuring the unit and verifying successful call placement and call reception.

Investigation from Field Notes and Service Engineering Team: (As per the Salesforce and Conversation with the Field Technician)

* Reviewed field service communication and technician notes from the on-site investigation.
* Verified that after the customer replaced the unit, the replacement device was initially unable to obtain an IP address.
* Confirmed with the field technician that on-site IT and FST investigated the connected port and PoE/network path.
troubleshooting_results: The returned original GRS10H device did not have any fault during the bench testing. It was configured on the ECT Server. Same firmware was used on RCB3 and GRS7 as that of GRS10H. The device was able to be configured and was able to place and receive calls in the lab environment. When the hospital received the new device, it initially could not obtain the IP Address until the network port issue was cleared by the Hospital IT Team. After the port/network condition was corrected, the replacement device was configured and used successfully. These findings do not support a hardware failure of the returned original device.

investigation_details: * Code blue lever is broken.

* It is noticeable when the code lever is pulled down that it is broken, which is the main reason why the device would not ring the code blue calls.
* After opening up the device it was observed that the code blue lever is broken from the plastic support itself. Since this device is 10+ years old, the code lever can break if handled roughly.

![](blob:https://media.staging.atl-paas.net/?type=file&localId=38f512e0c4f2&id=9f3f913f-6a5d-4c53-a365-e6adb4656af1&&collection=&height=6144&occurrenceKey=null&width=8160&__contextId=null&__displayType=null&__external=false&__fileMimeType=null&__fileName=null&__fileSize=null&__mediaTraceId=null&url=null)
troubleshooting_steps: Issue: Customer reports having issues with the code blue call, when they pull the code lever it does not annunciate.  
Date/Time: 08/07/2026  
GRS10 IP Address: 10.101.97.134  
Customer troubleshooting: None.

verification_summary: Verification activities confirmed that the Code Blue annunciation failure was isolated to the mechanical Code Blue lever assembly on P/N: P2594NNC2C11, S/N: 0331525FWIS. Inspection revealed that the lever had broken away from its plastic support, preventing the Code Blue call from being initiated. Functional testing verified that the device remained operational, configurable through the ECT, and capable of processing all other call types as expected. The physical condition of the lever supports the identified root cause and is consistent with damage resulting from rough handling, impact, or age-related wear. The findings confirm that the reported issue was caused by a hardware failure of the Code Blue lever assembly. No additional system failures were identified, and no patient injury or adverse event was reported.

title: Lost Primary or Secondary Audio Station
text: ## Problem

---

Used when there is a Lost Primary Audio Station or Lost Secondary Audio Station system alert on the primary console and in the Enterprise Configuration Tool's (ECT) 'Active Calls' section.

- Environment: Nurse Call - All versions
- This KB may require an RCB reboot

## Solution

---

1. Determine the audio station type, serial number and RCB port number by performing the following steps:
    1. On the GRS10 console navigate to Menu → System Alerts.
    2. Highlight the **Lost Audio Station** alert and click the **Show Details** button.
    3. At the bottom of the screen note if the Audio station is a GRS5 *(gas)* or SRS *(sas)*, its serial number and RCB Port number.

         For example:*** iob-0xxxxxxxWIS:gas-0xxxxxxxWIS:1*** - where ***iob-*** is RCB serial, ***gas-*** is GRS5 serial and ***:1*** or ***:2*** represent RCB ports that the audio station is connected to - RS1 or RS2 respectively.  
  
    4. If SRS, skip to **step 6**.  
    5. If GRS5 proceed to the next step.  
  
2. Determine if GRS5 is powered on or off, online or offline by performing the following steps:
    1. [Access the command line interface (CLI) of the parent RCB device](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/888144057/How+to+connect+to+a+base+device+command+line+interface+CLI) (parent of the lost GRS5).
    2. Once at *iob *command prompt, use *ping* command. If GRS5 is in port 1 use *10.0.0.2* IP address, if in port 2 use *10.0.0.6.*
    3. If ping was unsuccessful, skip to **step 5.**
    4. If ping was successful, the GRS5 is powered on and online; proceed to the next step.  
  
3. Determine if the GRS5 is properly configured and on the correct software version by performing the following steps:
    1. [Access the CLI of the GRS5](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/907903288/How+to+Access+GRS5+GRS7+Command+Line+Interface+CLI).
    2. Once at the  `gas-xxxxxwis $`command prompt, determine if the serial number in the prompt matches the serial number from **step 1.b**.
        1. If serial numbers are mismatched, make the necessary corrections in ECT.
        2. If they are the same, proceed to the next step.
    3. In the command prompt of the GRS, type ***nnc -v*** and hit enter. Note the application software version of the GRS5.
    4. Open Service Portal or SAMM Tool and determine if GRS5 is on the correct software version with the rest of the devices.
        1. If the software is mismatched, download and apply the correct version to the GRS5.
        2. If the software matches proceed to the next step.  
  
4. [Reboot the GRS5 and the parent RCB](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/1030848709/How+To+Reboot+a+Base+Device) and wait up to 5 min for the alerts to clear.
    1. If the system alert has cleared, complete the CRM resolution fields using the tables below. If issue persists, engage a senior member of your team for further guidance before escalating.  
    2. If the system alert persists, **replace the GRS5**.  
  
5. If ping was unsuccessful, perform the following steps to determine if the GRS5 is powered off or offline.
    1. Power down the parent RCB and test cabling between RCB and GRS5 and visually inspect both ports for damage.
    2. If cable tests passed and no port damage is seen, temporarily swap RS1 and RS2 ports on the RCB and power on the RCB to determine if power is being delivered to GRS5 on the other port.
        1. If power is being delivered to GRS5 and both RS ports are being used, the RCB has a faulty RS port and it needs to be replaced.
        2. If RS2 port was open, configure the GRS5 for port 2 in ECT and publish configuration.
        3. If GRS5 still does not power on, **replace the GRS5**.  
  
6. SRS’s are not IP addressable so no ping command can be performed from its parent RCB to verify the connectivity. A simple way to confirm connectivity of an SRS is to try a PSoC software download to the SRS in Service Portal or SAMM Tool.
    1. If PSoC download is unsuccessful, skip to **step 8**.
    2. If PSoC download is successful the SRS is powered on and online. Proceed to the next step.  
  
7. In Service Portal or SAMM Tool, determine if SRS is on the correct PSoC software version.
    1. If the software matches, try rebooting the SRS via Room Reset on GRS10 or by [rebooting its parent RCB](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/1030848709/How+To+Reboot+a+Base+Device).
    2. If none of the above fixes the issue, **replace the SRS**.  
  
8. If PSoC download was unsuccessful, perform the following steps to determine if the the SRS is powered off or offline.
9. If confirmed, complete the CRM resolution fields using the table below. If issue persists, engage a senior member of your team for further guidance before escalating.

## Cause

---

Misconfigured device  
Mismatched software versions  
Faulty cabling  
Faulty RCB RS port  
Faulty device

## Investigational summary fields

---

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| If **correcting ****configuration of** **GRS5 or SRS** resolved your issue, use these values to close the case |  |
| Main - Sub Assembly | Problem/Resolution Reason |
| Navicare Nurse Call (NNC) : Enterprise Configuration Tool (ECT) Voalte Nurse Call : Enterprise Configuration Tool (ECT) | Device Settings Misconfigured |

  

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| If **correcting mismatched device**** software version** resolved your issue, use these values to close the case |  |
| Main - Sub Assembly | Problem/Resolution Reason |
| Navicare Nurse Call (NNC) : GRS5 or SRS Voalte Nurse Call : GRS5 or SRS | Software Version Mismatch |

  

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| If **correcting device cabling **resolved your issue, use these values to close the case |  |
| Main - Sub Assembly | Problem/Resolution Reason |
| Navicare Nurse Call (NNC) : GRS5 or SRS Voalte Nurse Call : GRS5 or SRS | Port/Connector/Cable Damaged or Disconnected/Unplugged or Failure |

root_cause_summary: Root cause is blown diode D2_PWR which is a known issue for this SRS model/revision. This issue has been resolved in subsequent models and revisions (reference CRCO# C134673).
investigation_details: **HW Investigation**

Device arrived dead. Would not power up because +5V rail was shorted to Ground. Root cause is a blown diode D2_PWR, which is the catch diode for the 5V buck converter. For the P2594NNC1B11 with PCB BOM Agile PN: 164760 Rev 2, the D2_PWR component is a 60V part (MPN: LT1766EFE#TRPBF, Mfr: Linear Technology). Rev 3 of the PCB BOM contains the replacement parts which are rated at 100V – so the issue with this component was fixed by 2015/2016 model year and subsequent models (reference CRCO# C134673).

I found one similar case with this same version of the SRS (P2594NNC1B11):

* SN: 481309JWIS, NCMR0396716, Case: 23988 -- received/tested 14 June 2022
* Troubleshooting notes: “SRS is dead, no +5V. Catch diode, D2_PWR, short.  Known issue with this diode which has been corrected with alternate diode.”

Also worth noting is that the nurse station did receive a Lost Primary Audio Station Alert for ED1 and it was showing on the console prior to the Code Blue, see case in Salesforce. Therefore, the device was not functioning properly prior to the Code Blue event. Furthermore, the customer said they thought they had a pending ticket on their end to replace the device.

The site also had another SRS the month before that they asked for a replacement, serial number indicated it was the same week/year as the device for this case (04414089WIS). They rebooted the associated RCB device and the lost primary audio station alert was still present. Services team reached out multiple times to see if the replacement that was sent was installed and configured successfully for ED4 but received no response from the customer so that case (01040763) was eventually closed.

I replaced the D2_PWR with a working component and the device now passes FCT. Note that logs say partial fail because the VPD read/write test was skipped and the handset off hook test initially failed because I did not remove the handset from the FCT cradle in time and had to re-run the test – which passed on the second attempt.

root_cause_summary: Broken Code Lever probably due to rough handling of the device or a fall.
investigation_details: * Code blue lever is broken.
* Other than that, the device is up and running and configurable on the ECT. All calls other than code blue work as expected.
* It is noticeable when the code lever is pulled down that it is broken, which is the main reason why the device would not ring the code blue calls.
* After opening up the device it was observed that the code blue lever is broken from the plastic support itself. Since this device is 10+ years old, the code lever can break if handled roughly.

![](blob:https://media.staging.atl-paas.net/?type=file&localId=38f512e0c4f2&id=9f3f913f-6a5d-4c53-a365-e6adb4656af1&&collection=&height=6144&occurrenceKey=null&width=8160&__contextId=null&__displayType=null&__external=false&__fileMimeType=null&__fileName=null&__fileSize=null&__mediaTraceId=null&url=null)
troubleshooting_steps: Issue: Customer reports having issues with the code blue call, when they pull the code lever it does not annunciate.  
Date/Time: 08/07/2026  
GRS10 IP Address: 10.101.97.134  
Customer troubleshooting: None.   
Additional information: They found the issue accidentally. No patient outcome reported.
verification_summary: Verification activities confirmed that the Code Blue annunciation failure was isolated to the mechanical Code Blue lever assembly on P/N: P2594NNC2C11, S/N: 0331525FWIS. Inspection revealed that the lever had broken away from its plastic support, preventing the Code Blue call from being initiated. Functional testing verified that the device remained operational, configurable through the ECT, and capable of processing all other call types as expected. The physical condition of the lever supports the identified root cause and is consistent with damage resulting from rough handling, impact, or age-related wear. The findings confirm that the reported issue was caused by a hardware failure of the Code Blue lever assembly. No additional system failures were identified, and no patient injury or adverse event was reported.
rca_review_comments: Broken Code Lever probably due to rough handling of the device or a fall.  Device is past it’s useful life.

case_summary.summary: At Inova Fairfax Hospital, a GRS7 touch screen in North Tower 6th floor Room 646 froze and the code blue lever did not activate. Remote checks found no system alerts and a Chronos query showed no code blue or other call triggered from the room during the event window, so the customer replaced the GRS7, and the new unit responded properly to touch inputs.

case_summary.product: GRS7, Nurse Call system
case_summary.actions_taken: VNC'd into the room's GRS10 unit and found no system alerts on the console.
Checked RCB3 and GRS7 uptime and VOIP extension status via command line, all showing normal status.
VNC'd into the GRS7 and found it responsive to remote inputs.
Ran a Chronos query for the room covering the event window, finding no code blue or other call triggered.
Applied software to a new GRS7 and swapped the device serial in ECT configuration.
Added a later Chronos query result showing a successful code lever test despite the screen being frozen.
case_summary.resolution: Replaced the GRS7; the new unit responded properly to touch inputs.
case_summary.status: resolved

description: Property is alleging that a code blue call did not annunciate and that it had a frozen screen. When the code blue was tested with our Nursecall T1 team the code lever worked as designed. Device had not been rebooted since the alleged event.
root_cause_summary: The GRS7 screen was frozen at the time of incident due to known frozen screen defect present in GRS7 application versions prior to 4.1.200.

Because the screen was unresponsive, the customer's attempt to place an emergency call via on screen button did not register, no corresponding event was logged. Per Technical Support's conversation with the customer and confirmed by log evidence, the physical code lever was never pulled; had it been, a call log entry would have been generated immediately regardless of the screen's frozen state, since the code lever is hardware-driven and independent of the touchscreen UI/app.
investigation_details: here's what I've looked for so far:
1. looking in Chronos for call activity (none)
2. Looking in the provided Call table records for call activity from the route ids for the grs7 and rcb (none) -- one thing: on 9/12 the rcb was reported lost (lost rcb system alert)
3. looked thru advanced svc logs for any references to rcb or grs7 (by serial number) -- nothing out of the ordinary other than the grs7 was reported off-line (by bmsproxy) at 03:30ish for 20 minutes on 9/14
4. looked thru syslogs for any references to rcb or grs7 (by serial number) -- nothing out of the ordinary
**Update** 9/25/2026: 
* Timeline of events during the day of incident according to the logs:
| **Date/Time** | **Event** | **Interpretation** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 9/12/202617:22 | GRS7 040241FYWM2 and connected RCB3 043240DRWM2 logged watchdog shutdown/restart activity. | About two days before the incident; not evidence of failure during the day of incident |
| 9/14/202607:33 | GRS7 logged an ASBC call, call-type - 31 (Normal Call) GRS-7 logged call type \[9\]- Bed Offline | Bed-related call event; not a code blue Bed power was disconnected while the 37-PIN Connector stayed on. |
| 9/14/20267:35 | GRS-7 logged call type \[7\] - Bed Disconnect | 37-PIN Connector was removed and bed was probably moved out. |
| 9/14/20267:38 | RCB3 registered a VOIP call and was put on hold. | Call was a result of Call Type \[7\] - Bed Disconnect Call. |
| 9/14/20267:56-7:57 | GRS7 logged ASBC connected. | Bed was connected back to the room and Alerts were cancelled. |
| 9/14/20268:07-8:09 | GRS7 logged call type \[9\] was created and cancelled. | Bed Exit Alert; probably was cancelled after caregiver attention. |
| 9/14/202610:38 | GRS7 registered that the call that was on hold was cancelled after 3 hours. | **Other observation and activity** |
Between `8:00 AM to 9:00 AM` EST the RCB3 and the GRS7 showed `nnc: -- MARK --` in the log every 20 minutes. This proves that the nnc-app was active and did not die or reboot.
Also bed exit alarm ringing was not cancelled from the grs7 but was cancelled from the bed itself which is why it kept going off every 30 seconds. 
Update 9/29/2026: 
* Based on the evidence and conversation with the TS it was found that the customer did not pull the code lever, but they tried to press the emergency button on the screen. This is also evident from the logs that code lever was never pulled down as an immediate log is generated for the same even if the screen is frozen.

comment_summary: At a customer site, GRS7 devices became unresponsive to touch while the room otherwise functioned normally, with calls and audio working. On an affected room where the RCB and GRS7 had been up for 55 days, evtest confirmed the Atmel touchscreen was still present, yet the screen would not respond or wake, and the display returned to normal only after the room was rebooted from the GRS10. Unlike a similar issue elsewhere, there was no widespread rebooting at this site and devices typically stayed online for 100 days or more, so the thread treats it as a different problem, while suggesting the investigational patch from the other investigation might help because it removes a sleep message sent in some scenarios. After the site was upgraded to Nursecall 4.200, a new support ticket reported the same GRS7 touchscreen freezes plus an inability to hang up calls from the GRS7 without rebooting from the GRS10.

root_cause_summary: Root cause for failure --> the excessive force applied by the user of \~ 25N led to the failure. verification_summary: GRS7 and GRS5 devices were subjected to force tests in the back/side/down positions to measure when the code lever fails. They were able to simulate the breaking of the code blue lever in a similar manner to the returned devices and found that the lever is weaker when pulling to the side. This is not a normal user scenario.

Summary: No design failures were identified as it was difficult to break the code lever during normal user  
Scenario.
rca_review_comments: Excessive is the root cause here.  GRS7 code Levers has been tested at 100k cycles, with no failure and therefore if normal force is used the lever should not fail.

comment_summary: A reported Code Blue that did not alert could not be replicated in the lab on 26FEB2025, where the call registered and was placed as intended using the code lever. The web relay, which had been returned in the box but not initially investigated, was tested in a separate QE lab set-up and found to be working as intended, so replication would require its exact configuration at the customer site, including PoE model and port load, RCB2/RCB3, the returned GRS5 and any GRS10/GRS10H. title: Inoperable Touch Screen on GRS10/GRS10H or GRS5/GRS7
text: ## Problem

---

The screen on a GRS5/GRS7 or GRS10/10H is frozen or not responding correctly to user input.

- Environment: Nurse Call - GRS10/GRS10H and GRS5/GRS7 devices only!
- This KB may require a GRS10/10H reboot
- This KB may require a GRS5/GRS7 reboot
- This KB requires onsite help
- There are currently two RCAs opened to investigate GRS7 touchscreen failure
    - [RCA-1272 - Touchscreen driver missing and/or device is rebooting](https://hill-rom.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1272)
    - [RCA-1311 - Touchscreen unresponsive, but driver is present. Device is not rebooting](https://hill-rom.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1311)
    - If it is determined to be one of these defects an upgrade to 4.1.200 or higher is required to permanently resolve this issue.

## Solution

---

1. Check the active calls window in [ECT](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/914555355/How+to+Open+ECT) or the primary console, and determine if there are any active lost \<device\> system alerts for the affected device.
    1. If there are, refer to [Lost Primary Console/Lost Secondary Console](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/2629861616/Lost+NUC+Lost+Primary+Console+and+Lost+Secondary+Console) or [Lost Primary/Secondary Audio Station](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/2629730338/Lost+Primary+or+Secondary+Audio+Station) article to resolve the issue. 
    2. If there are no active system alerts for the affected device proceed to the next step.
2. If the screen is completely frozen and not responding to user input please proceed to the specific instructions for the device you are working with below


## GRS-5/GRS-10 Solution  

---

If the device screen is frozen/non-responsive, the device might fail the recalibration procedure below, and brick!

Only when a spare device is available, proceed to the next step.


The next steps reboot the device. The device will then require manual calibration input from the end user.  
Ensure that the end user is available to help before proceeding. Proceeding with this step will result in a temporary lost device system alert, preventing it from booting up fully until the screen is calibrated.

## WinSCP Method (Recommended)

1. Follow the steps on the linked page for [removal of the device pointercal file using WinSCP](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/917602986/How+to+remove+the+pointercal+file+via+WinSCP).

## CLI Method (Use only if WinSCP cannot be installed or used)  
  

1. For GRS-5 using CLI:
    1. [Access the GRS5 command line interface](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/907903288/How+to+Access+GRS5+GRS7+Command+Line+Interface+CLI).
    2. Navigate to the **/data/etc** directory by typing `cd /data/etc`  and proceed to the next step.
    3. Remove the ‘pointercal' file by typing `rm -rf pointercal`  and proceed to the next step.
    4. Reboot the device by typing `reboot`
2. For GRS-10 using CLI :
    1. [Access the GRS10 command line interface](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/888144057/How+to+connect+to+a+base+device+command+line+interface+CLI).
    2. Navigate to the **/data/etc** directory by typing `cd /data/etc`  and proceed to the next step.
    3. Remove the ‘pointercal’ file by typing `rm -rf pointercal`  and proceed to the next step.
    4. Reboot the device by typing `reboot`

## Calibrate Touch Screen

1. When the device powers back on, instruct the end user to calibrate the screen by touching the 5 crosshairs as they appear on the screen.

If the screen calibration is not performed in a timely manner, the device will eventually enter **Recovery Mode** and will have to be rebooted to repeat the process at Step 4.
2. Wait for the device to finish booting up and test the touch screen.
3. If confirmed, complete the SalesForce resolution fields using the table below. If issue persists, replace the device.

## GRS-7 Solution  

---

GRS-7 utilizes a capacitive touchscreen controller.  The touchscreen controller's driver is loaded upon startup of the device and does not rely on a **pointercal** file to maintain calibration.   
  
If the touchscreen of the GRS-7 is non-responsive or misaligned, validate touchscreen drivers are missing then perform a soft reboot of the device.

1. For GRS-7 using CLI:
    1. [Access the GRS7 command line interface](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/907903288/How+to+Access+GRS5+GRS7+Command+Line+Interface+CLI).
    2. To determine if this is related to either **RCA-1272** or **RCA-1311**, check the status of the touchscreen drivers by typing **sudo evtest** at the command prompt  
  
**RCA-1272: ** */dev/input/event1* missing

         
  
**RCA-1311:  ***/dev/input/event1* present

       
    3. Exit evtest mode by typing **Ctrl + C** 
    4. Reboot the device by typing **sudo reboot**
2. Wait for the device to finish booting up and test the touch screen.
    1. If the issue persists, have onsite help physically disconnect the power supply from the device until it shuts down.  Reconnect the power supply
    2. Reconnect and allow to power up
3. Wait for the device to finish booting up and test the touch screen. 
4. Use the CLI
    1. [Access the GRS7 command line interface](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/CTS/pages/907903288/How+to+Access+GRS5+GRS7+Command+Line+Interface+CLI).
    2. Confirm the touchscreen drivers are now present by typing **sudo evtest**

5. If confirmed, complete the SalesForce resolution & Complaint Qualification Investigation ID fields using the table below.
6. If issue persists, replace the device.

summary: Bed exit alarm not ringing on GRS10 - 2 RCB's returned
description: Additional information (as the customer stated in the original email): I believe those rooms are in the same groups, please check settings. You can compare to bed 366, this is ringing correctly to GRS10.  
Patient Impact(yes/no): The customer mentioned in the original email that this is a safety issue.
root_cause_summary: The issue was confirmed in Rooms 359 and 361. During testing, the bed-exit alarms were delayed and took longer than expected to clear, and continuous ping testing showed repeated timeouts. The system logs also show similar communication failures affecting multiple unrelated devices connected to the same service host. This points more toward an intermittent network or service-host communication problem than a confirmed RCB hardware failure.

Replacing the RCB2 units with RCB3 units restored normal operation, but the replacement also included software installation, device serialization, ECT configuration, VOIP setup, and clearing the lost-device alerts. Because several changes were made at the same time, the replacement alone does not prove that the original RCBs were defective. 

Both returned RCBs also passed Bed Exit alarm testing on the bench. Based on the available evidence, the most likely cause was an intermittent field communication or service-host issue. A permanent hardware failure in either RCB has not been demonstrated.
investigation_details: **Software Investigation:**
* Bench tested on of the returned RCB (31130NAWIS) with a GRS5 and a GRS10H and manually triggered a bed exit alarm, it rang correctly on the GRS10H and the GRS5.
* **On-site (as mentioned on Salesforce), TS found continuous ping timeouts to both RCBs** during the original screen-share investigation, with alarms "slow to alarm and slow to clear." Since the units test clean on bench, root cause is more likely related to **site network conditions** (switch/VLAN/PoE/latency) than to the RCB hardware itself.
* No ping timeouts were observed on the RCB during the bench testing.
* _Note: the site fix involved full de-registration/re-registration (remove old RCB, add new RCB to NUC, re-serialize) in addition to a physical swap. Given bench testing shows the returned RCBs function correctly, it's possible the fix resulted from re-registration/network reseat rather than a hardware defect in the RCB itself. Bed exit GRS10 ringing was never explicitly retested onsite postfix, only 2-way audio was confirmed._
**~~Possible Next Steps:~~**
* **~~Configuration is still an open variable~~** ~~- the customer's original hypothesis was that the affected rooms (359/361) may not share the same GRS10 paging/annunciation group as the working comparison room (366). This has not yet been verified against the site's ECT config and should be compared directly.~~
* ~~Testing of the second RCB unit is still pending.~~
Update 9/22/2026:
* Syslogs were fetched from the server:
 * The returned devices are RCBs with the following log identifiers:
 * RCB serial `31330TJWIS` appears in the syslogs as `031130TJWIS` / host `iob-031130TJWIS`.
 * RCB serial `31130NAWIS` appears in the syslogs as `031130NAWIS` / host `iob-031130NAWIS`.
* Both RCBs were bench tested after return. Bed Exit alarm functionality operated correctly during bench testing. No ping timeouts either.
* From the syslogs it is evident that there was a network issue which caused the RCBs to go down, which caused its child devices to also not respond to the network.
verification_summary: Based on the available evidence, no hardware failure was identified in the returned RCBs. Results support the conclusion that the reported condition was most likely the result of an intermittent network or service-host communication disruption within the site environment. The complaint condition was not reproduced during returned-product testing, and the performance of the returned devices was verified to be within specification.
rca_review_comments: Intermittent network or service-host communication problem than a confirmed RCB hardware failure.

comment_summary: ECT reported "Transfer Session ### already exists" errors and failing configuration pushes for three rooms, even though Config service logs showed the RCB and GRS5s in those rooms receiving ConfigUpdate and Apply messages and acknowledging correctly. The transfer session IDs in the error details referenced old device IDs that were no longer configured for those locations, and those devices' IP addresses from the NavicareEnterprise database were unreachable from the advanced server. The initial theory was that the GRS5s were still stored in the database with their old, unreachable IP addresses, with a proposed cleanup of historic devices. * Hall 02-03 | RCB - 22507RWM2 | GRS7 - 512516YWM2
* Hall 07-08 | RCB - 7250UUWM2 | GRS7 - 512516TWM2
* Hall 13-14 | RCB - 7250EVWM2 | GRS7 - 5125135WM2



The only thing that looks out of place is these three locations are sharing and RCB with a patient room. Even with a unit override for staff stations to ALWAYS tone on normal calls these 3 duty stations still will not tone until they are rebooted. They noted they have a 4th duty station in the unit that never has this issue. Treatment hall. investigation_details: I turned up TONESVC logging to the highest level on 4 duty stations - the duty station 10.12.62.188 that is working as expected, as well as the 3 duty stations where toning was reported to not work:

I pushed configuration by changing the room to room audio timer by 1 second in system options.  Also I rebooted each of these three stations.

After a few weeks, the logging indicates the stations are playing tones.  The customer reports the stations are working.

It is possible there was old config on the boards.

Initial report: GRS10s are beeping with no calls or alerts active. Calls are also being stuck on child devices. All of this began post last upgrade to 4.2.

Current status: After purging the configuration on the effected GRS10s the beeping with no active calls ceased. Has not returned yet but this is the second iteration of the customer having a GRS10 toning without having an active call/alert. The calls getting stuck on the child devices don’t follow normal procedure for placing and cancelling calls. See troubleshooting summary.  
  
Request: Confirm why GRS10s are having this beeping issue with no active calls/alerts.

Confirm why calls are getting stuck on child devices.
comment_summary: A site reported GRS10s emitting a three-tone beeping noise with no active calls or alerts, together with sporadic stuck calls where a call placed in one room remained active on a GRS5 in another room with no matching active call in the database. Raising APLMOD logging to level 7 on an affected RCB confirmed a tone being played repeatedly with no reference to a current call, and the stuck call cleared after rebooting the room; purging the configuration of a GRS10 resolved a beeping instance. The pattern identified was that affected calls were all configured "display at patient station: always", only old hardware was involved (GRS5 not GRS7, RCB not RCB3, AGAS not GRS10H), and it occurred in units where an AGAS acts as the NUC, suggesting a timing issue. Replacing the AGAS NUC with an RCB3 NUC in an affected unit stopped recurrences there and the approach was extended to other units, while merely turning logging up also appeared to change the timing and stop the problem; the thread concludes it is a timing issue with no single identifiable cause, expected to be corrected by the significant changes in 4.2.200.

root_cause_summary: This is a timing issue.  And, while we can’t point at anyting and say “this is the cause”, things have changed significantly in 4.2.200 which is expected to correct the issue. https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-386#icft=NC-386 is the item the work was done under.  

[https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-386](https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-386)
investigation_details: have been looking thru logs and looking at devices where this has happened.   
  
characteristics:

1. call is placed, annunciates normally and is eventually canceled.  Call remains active on a GRS5
2. the common characteristics for call configuration so far is that they have all been “display at patient station: always”
3. only has been observed on old hardware: grs5, not grs7, rcb, not rcb3, agas not grs10h
4. happens in units that have an AGAS as a nuc
5. seems to be some sort of timing issue, this could also be a coincidence, turning up logging on devices for a unit where this happens as frequently as anywhere, which is still very infrequently, and it has not happened in that unit since.

Hospital has been adding an rcb3 nuc to units where this has happened and we have not seen a re-occurrence in those units since.
troubleshooting_steps: Received call from Sam Gormont around 8:45 am. Called Sam back. He confirmed the issue has returned with GRS10 beeping with no calls/alerts.  
Requested he confirm what console he is at. He gave the ip address 172.16.26.1 which belongs to the GRS10 NUC for 3 North.  
Further probing revealed the beeping was related to a accurate bed offline alert. Walked Sam through steps for checking call.  
Cleared alert after adjusting power cable for bed. Confirmed now we have no beeping.  
Confirmed beeping with no active calls or alerts has not reoccured since purging config consoles.  
Sam then brought up another stuck call on a GRS5. GRS5 for room W 362 is showing a call from room N 376.  
This call has been on the waitlist for 52 hours. Vnc into both GRS5s. Confirmed N 376 does not show a active call.  
Restarted messaging service on the off chance nursefollower issue could have applied. No change. Restarted Device service. No change.  
While the device service was down the GRS5 for W 362 never rebooted any alerts. It also still held on to the stuck normal call.  
Resetting audio did nothing. Placed another normal call from N 376 to W 362. Our existing normal call is the only call that shows.  
Although audio does still open between the two as of we accepted a call that we never receive. Sam did confirm he can hear the feedback on the audio station confirming audio is open.  
When checking the syslogs for evidence of audio being opened between the two devices. Did not find a voip transaction for the call.  
Sam confirmed rebooting the effected room will fix it but it will return. Requested we reboot to clear and try to replicate.  
Rebooted room W 362. Confirmed now call is cleared. Placed another normal call from N 376. No call ever appeared although audio does open still without being accepted.  
Sam confirmed this has only been a issue since upgrading. He stated prior to the upgrade they rarely had a open Nursecall case. Now they have frequent cases surrounding stuck calls.  
Confirmed i would continue to investigate but this will likely need a RCA. Sam confirmed. Checked software version for all devices. Confirmed they are all on the correct version.  
Site does have multiple lost secondary alerts. Thought this was related to a down CCD/PBX. Did not find a CCD/PBX for the site. Further probing revealed the site has multiple unserialized devices connected.
troubleshooting_results: Call is cleared but customer would like confirmation on why they are getting stuck.
verification_summary: Identified Tech Story https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-386#icft=NC-386 to address WebSocket issues. Fix planned for 4.2.200 software release.

description: GRS7 to GRS10 calls worked but GRS7 to Linq was not working. We ran into a similar issue on 1/13/26 and had to reboot ER room 2. This was the 3rd time we rebooted ER2 to be able to get Linq calls to work. Pending more thorough testing on specific use cases
comment_summary: A site sporadically could not call a particular Linq device: Nurse Call to Nurse Call audio worked, Linq to Linq audio worked, and other stations could call the same badge, but one specific station to that Linq badge failed until the audio station was rebooted. Diagnostic steps were supplied to run fs_cli.exe -p voalte against the FreeSWITCH service on the Nurse Call Enterprise server to see whether RTC was routing the audio setup request to Nurse Call at all, with SIP-level tracing as the next step if it was. Because audio paths within Nurse Call, within Linq, and between them all worked, and because rebooting the audio station resolved it by forcing a re-download of staff wireless configuration, the theory settled on the audio station holding incorrect dialing information for that staff member, as happens when a staff member is assigned a Linq badge while CSA configuration in ECT is incorrect, since wireless device configuration updates do not trigger a staff mobile device assignment update. The site reported no known Wireless Device changes in ECT near the event, Gateway logs were not set to Verbose so data was limited, the issue was never reproducible, and no further occurrences were reported after an upgrade.

The datastore also restored did not have the Database Master Key, the Navicare Certificate, or the Navicare Symmetric Key required for column level encryption. The post restore is linking that chain to the new OS → SQL Instance piece.

summary: ERM - Symmetric key error running post-restore utility after ERM restore
description: Creating RCA per request of Shannon Santana

Performing ERM migration.  Requirement is to backup warehouse, master and all datastore DB’s from old ERM SQL server and then restore to new ERM SQL server.  After restore, required to run Post-restore database utility.  During processing for datastore, Symmetric key error is encountered.



**Environment:**  Windows 2019,  VNC 4.0.404, ERM 4.7



**Solution:**  escalate to R&D to created manually create encryption key in original datastore DB.  After manual key is created, backup and restore datastore db, then proceed with post-restore utility.

Encryption key is created in initial setup of datastore.  In some instances key is not created.  No error is produced when this happens and ERM functions as expected.  The key does not effect functionality of ERM, only effects the ability to restore the datastore.
root_cause_summary: The datastore database on the existing server does not have the database master key, the encryption certificate, or the symmetric key required for column level encryption.
investigation_details: * ERM migrations require datastore databases to be backed up, restored, and then processed using the post-restore database utility. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* The datastore database on the existing server lacked the Database Master Key, encryption certificate, and symmetric key used for column-level encryption. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* During post-restore processing, the utility expected these encryption objects to exist and failed when they could not be found. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* Investigation determined that the encryption key should normally be created during the initial datastore setup, but in certain installations the key creation process did not occur and no error was generated at the time. [\[RCA-1260 | Word\]](https://myfiles.baxter.com/personal/matt_tague_baxter_com/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7B91485DE7-BCA5-4153-9705-2C26D8C14A83%7D&file=RCA-1260.doc&action=default&mobileredirect=true)
* Because the missing keys do not affect normal ERM operations, the issue remained hidden until a datastore restore or migration was attempted.
verification_summary: Record-review verification summary: Based on the existing Jira investigation, root-cause, review, and comment records. This summary documents previously recorded evidence; no new functional testing or independent verification was performed.

The investigation identified missing datastore encryption objects—Database Master Key, encryption certificate and symmetric key—as the cause of ERM post-restore processing failure. The documented remediation is controlled escalation to database specialists to create the missing objects before repeating backup/restore and the post-restore utility. The RCA records creation/approval of a KB and a review of three affected sites, without a common version/configuration factor. These records support the failure mechanism and documented support pathway, but contain no explicit completed post-remediation restore test or result. Successful post-restore processing remains to be evidenced for final effectiveness verification. Basis: Description, Investigation Details, Root Cause Summary and 26 April 2024 comment.

=== Case ===
CaseNumber: 00965986
Reported software version: Voalte Nurse Call 4.1.210
case_summary.summary: Specific users at the site were unable to receive calls on their wireless mobile devices, alongside related issues with calls not cancelling and ringing after callback. Investigation found an oversized message header (over 1499 bytes, caused by extended names in the P-Location field) forcing an additional codec, compounded by competing SIP traffic on the customer's network; a prior SIC version rollback and user role/profile corrections also factored into restoring calls. The issues were addressed through a SIC version rollback, packet/header-related fixes, and building a dedicated SIP location for the site.
case_summary.reported_issue: Specific users were unable to receive Nurse Call alerts on their wireless mobile devices, and calls were not cancelling or were ringing devices after callback.
case_summary.product: Wireless/mobile call delivery (FreeSWITCH, SIP/Avaya integration)
case_summary.actions_taken: Reviewed call type and wait list configuration for affected call types
Rolled back the Connexall SIC (Standard Input Client) from version 8.0.16 to 8.0.7, which corrected calls ringing devices after callback
Adjusted Cancel Patient Call and Reminder List Timer settings on multiple servers
Tested bathroom request and pain meds calls and adjusted latching and reminder list timer settings
Reassigned a user's device and changed her role from CNA to PCA in Voalte Admin to troubleshoot a call-delivery failure
Baxter identified packet header irregularities causing an extra codec to be used for affected users
Built a dedicated SIP location for the site to separate its SIP traffic from another site it had been sharing
case_summary.resolution: Packet headers were corrected to stay under the 1499-byte limit and a dedicated SIP location was built for the site to resolve SIP traffic contention, restoring call delivery to the affected devices.
case_summary.status: resolved
case_summary.key_points: Header size needed to stay under 1499 bytes; extended names in the P-Location field were pushing packets over that limit
Site's SIP traffic had been routed through another site with no location of its own
Rolling back SIC from 8.0.16 to 8.0.7 resolved a separate symptom of alerts dispatching after callback
Syslog, FreeSWITCH logs, and PCAPs were needed to find the exact problem

summary: No response from device to SIP invite for call-back
description: While attempting to implement a wireless messaging integration from Nurse Call 4.2.000 to Cerner iBus it was found that calls are not being established back to the Nurse Call device.
root_cause_summary: Sip invite packets exceed 1,499 bytes.
investigation_details: A wireshark trace of the sip port shows that the sip invite packet is 1,542 bytes long, and is therefore truncated to 1,499 bytes by our devices.

Our devices can only receive SIP udp packets that are 1499 bytes or less.
troubleshooting_steps: Messages are successfully being delivered to Cerner.  The end-user is able to choose “Accept and call-back”.  Cerner sends the SIP invite back to Nurse Call’s FreeSwitch via and Avaya PBX.  The PBX forwards the invite to FreeSwitch.  FreeSwitch is correctly translating the 5 digit alias to the internal serial number extension.  FreeSwitch is sending the invite to the correct IP address for that extension.
troubleshooting_results: The FreeSwitch logs and a Wireshark capture show the invite being sent to the device IP but there is no response.  I don’t even see an error message.
rca_review_comments: Extra lines in the sip invite packet must be removed to reduce the size of the packet to 1,499 bytes or less.

summary: NNC - 4.1.210 - Specific User Cannot Receive Calls on their Mobiles
description: Customer was upgraded to 4.1.200 at the beginning of the Month.  
  
Two specific users are unable to receive patient calls to their mobiles (IPhones via Connexall). It is only these two users, and it follows them between devices. Other users are able to grab their phones and be able to receive calls, communicate with patients, et al. Call flow is as follows:  
  
Patient Places Call => Phone Rings => Call is immediately closed by phone => Call Rings at Nurse Station

The customer has deleted both the users' Connexall profiles and their AD profiles, then recreated them to no effect. Once the profiles are recreated, the problem reoccurs. I've also had them keep the AD profiles, label them as old, and create them new profiles to work with, including export into Connexall’s systems with no success.

Wiresharks performed on a test call with the users experiencing the issue show that the call is connecting, but being closed within miliseconds by "mod_sofia", which FreeSWITCH documentation is identifying as the SIP endpoint ([https://developer.signalwire.com/freeswitch/FreeSWITCH-Explained/Modules/mod_sofia_1048707/).](https://developer.signalwire.com/freeswitch/FreeSWITCH-Explained/Modules/mod_sofia_1048707/).)  
  
Further examination of the packets do not show a reason as to why this is occurring, nor do our logs.  
  
Included files:  
\-Two wireshark captures, filtered down to the appropriate packets to show the point of failure (User With Issue) and a healthy call (User with No Issue)  
\-An image showing packet headers and bodies from the INVITE packets in both calls (“W” side for Working, “N” for Not)
root_cause_summary: The INVITE sip packet exceeds the allowable size limit of 1499 bytes.
investigation_details: A wireshark capture from the server showed that outgoing INVITE udp packets are exceeding the 1499 byte capacity of our base devices.    For some users, this will produce a **fatal** parse error in the base device sip stack (vocal), for other users (most of them) this produces an error that is not fatal and the call completes.
troubleshooting_steps: 1. Test calls have been run between both a user profile encountering the issue (there are only two) and a user that is working properly. Wiresharks were captured and examined, alongside logs. 
2. Customer deleted Connexall profile, then reimported it from AD.
3. Customer deleted AD profile, then recreated it.
troubleshooting_results: 1. Test Calls show point of failure, but nothing within the logs or the Wireshark captures show why.
2. Users still having issues
3. Users still having issues
verification_summary: Identified defect https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/NC-21509#icft=NC-21509, which will be assessed and considered for future software release.
rca_review_comments: The size of the INVITE udp header **must** be reduced, by either setting compact headers ON in freeswitch, or the customer reducing the size of their added headers.

description: * The customer has a wireless integration from Nurse Call to Connexall via Longleaf Relay
* The customer was upgraded from NNC 3.9.200 to Voalte NC 4.0.300 on 11/16/2021

| 4.5.550.5 | 4.0.300 | 2021/11/16 14:52:59 | NULL |

 

The customer alleges, and Sean Delaney the Director of Technical Services for Hillrom has confirmed, that prior to the upgrade, and going back several years, when a caregiver receives a normal priority Nurse Call alert on their wireless phone, they could choose to callback from the alert to a room device, and the alert cancels in Nurse Call.

Since the upgrade was completed callback from the wireless device no longer cancel the alert in Nurse Call.

 

The customer wants this functionality restored.  

I did want to add that I was curious if this was related to RCA-651 / Glue
root_cause_summary: The ability to cancel calls in previous versions was never intended, and is a patient safety risk, so that ability was removed.
investigation_details: Cancelling calls via wireless was an accidental bug, it was never an intended feature.   Due to patient safety reasons, that functionality was removed.
verification_summary: The cancellation of calls by wireless devices was a defect accidentally released to the field.  The code has been changed to move the calls to the reminder list instead of cancelling them.   Remote cancellation of calls by wireless devices is a patient safety risk.  
The accidentally released defect was fixed via https://hill-rom.atlassian.net/browse/GLUE-4228#icft=GLUE-4228.

root_cause_summary: Customer-site network/PoE port issue affecting device connectivity and operation. When tested on bench was not able to reproduce the issue. No hardware fault identified.
investigation_details: Customer initially reported that the GRS10H was unable to establish audio and displayed the error message “Temporary problem placing call please try again later.” The customer replaced the device locally in an attempt to resolve the issue. During the on-site follow-up, the replacement device was then found to be unable to obtain an IP address. Once the port issue was addressed on the customer side, the replacement device was able to obtain network connectivity, be configured, and operate successfully. The original returned device was later evaluated in R&D and no fault was reproduced. The unit configured normally and was able to place and receive calls on the bench.
troubleshooting_steps: FCT Logs Attached in the comments. FCT passed for all the hardware tests on this device.

R&D Investigation:

* Reviewed the reported issue on primary GRS10 at 10.23.186.207 after the customer observed the message “Temporary problem placing call, please try again later” when answering calls.
* Confirmed the customer had already verified all RCB ports and did not identify any port-level fault.
* Checked the GRS10 for active alarms, alerts, or other visible fault indications at the time of investigation.
* Attempted to validate the issue condition, but the behavior was not reproducible during review.
* Bench-tested the returned original device in R&D by configuring the unit and verifying successful call placement and call reception.

Investigation from Field Notes and Service Engineering Team: (As per the Salesforce and Conversation with the Field Technician)

* Reviewed field service communication and technician notes from the on-site investigation.
* Verified that after the customer replaced the unit, the replacement device was initially unable to obtain an IP address.
* Confirmed with the field technician that on-site IT and FST investigated the connected port and PoE/network path.
troubleshooting_results: The returned original GRS10H device did not have any fault during the bench testing. It was configured on the ECT Server. Same firmware was used on RCB3 and GRS7 as that of GRS10H. The device was able to be configured and was able to place and receive calls in the lab environment. When the hospital received the new device, it initially could not obtain the IP Address until the network port issue was cleared by the Hospital IT Team. After the port/network condition was corrected, the replacement device was configured and used successfully. These findings do not support a hardware failure of the returned original device.

summary: GRS5 Failed during Network Maintenance.
description: NCMR:  NCMR0446716

* QTY: 3
* GRS5 (PN: P2594NNC2D11)
* Serial Numbers: 

    * 041192LTWIS
    * 041192S2WIS
    * 0282006WWIS
    

Described Field Issue: 

During some regular network maintenance 3 x GRS5 failed and could not be powered on. The customer asserted this is not the first time this has happened and is asking why devices failed. 3 devices have been RMA’d back to understand what failed.

These are the GRS5; 0282006WWIS, 041192S2WIS, 041192LTWIS

1ZH920509025475593 is the tracking number for the RMA.

We have identified that the customer is not participating in LLDP on their POE’s and we have asked that they review their POE port settings but we are not sure if that would contribute to a failed device.
root_cause_summary: Two of the three have a crc error when loading both the kernel and recovery images, which indicates that whatever happened during the network maintenance must have caused a communication outage when these devices were in the middle of an update. The other one is in a crash loop.
investigation_details: Engineering Investigation Start Date: 04-MAY-2026

Hardware engineering Investigation Completion Date: 05-MAY-2026

Device Details:

* GRS5 P/N: P2594NNC2D11
* Refer to description section for device serial numbers.

HW Engineering Investigation Summary:

* The returned GRS5 units were tested to verify power functionality. All devices successfully powered ON without any issues. The operating system (OS) was able to boot; however, none of the units were able to launch or load the Nurse Call application software.
* This behavior indicates that the Nurse Call application loading process has been corrupted or compromised. The units appear to be stuck in a crash loop during application initialization.
* Touchscreen hardware functionality was not verified, as the devices did not progress far enough in the boot sequence to load the application.
* Testing was conducted using a HIB fixture environment. Refer to the attachments for corresponding serial numbers and captured boot-up screen information.
* SW team (Mark R.) will continue investigating for possible SW issues due to the application crashing, which can be due to several different things.
* Observations per device: (See attachment for images)

    * 0282006WWIS - Device powered ON and stayed at the ‘System entering recovery mode’ step. Application failed to load.
    * 041192S2WIS - Device powered ON and continuously kept rebooting to load the Application software. Application failed to load. 
    * 041192LTWIS -Device powered ON and failed to load application.   
        
    

SW Investigation:  
  
Two of the three have a crc error when loading both the kernel and recovery images, which indicates that whatever happened during the network maintenance must have caused a communication outage when these devices were in the middle of an update. The other one is in a crash loop.   
  
Customer had mentioned LLDP may have been implicated.   
Possible scenario:

During download/transfer of the software files the RCB was starved of voltage from its PoE port > The child device depends on the RCB for its source of power, so any power instability upstream causes a transient brown out condition for the device ultimately recieving the data.
troubleshooting_steps: Standard Lost Audio Station troubleshooting transpired without the ability to repair the devices.
troubleshooting_results: Replaced devices with newer GRS7’s.
verification_summary: Most likely a network outage while devices were in process of an update.
rca_review_comments: Inconclusive but potentially caused by network outage
