summary: NC - Basement PBX - Lost Unit Server
description: Customer details:

Acct # 605080

Acct name:Lubbock County Hospital District



Issue- PBX console (Secondary GRS10) was showing 30 lost unit server alerts. Unable to receive Code blue alerts. Checking performance of the GRS10 it remains at a constant 98/99% for CPU usage for NNC. 

Cause- The CPU usage is due to the GRS10 failing to make connections to other NNC devices over port 50005. Most of the connections show a TIME_WAIT instead of ESTABLISHED. Further probing revealed these connection failures was due to a disabled GRS10H NUC on the same subnet as our effected GRS10. 

Resolution: Rebooting the disabled GRS10H NUC resolved the issue of the failed connections on our effected GRS10. After the reboot connections were established and NNC CPU utilization on the GRS10 went down. 

Reason for RCA- We need to confirm why a disabled NUC would cause this sort of issue.
comment_summary: A basement PBX console reported Lost Unit Server alerts, together with high NNC CPU utilization on a GRS10 even though the bed plugins were not in use. Removing all plugins except calls and repeatedly rebooting the GRS10H NUC cut the alerts from 30 to 17 and finally cleared them, although the plugin-related spiking was supposed to have been resolved after 3.9.401. Later work found Lost Unit Server and lost secondary console alerts persisting for a nursing unit that was disabled in ECT, and the alerts cleared only after removing that disabled unit from the secondary unit monitoring of the other primary console and of the PBX. In the final session, re-enabling monitoring and rebooting the PBX no longer reproduced the alerts, and the engineer disabled SNTP on a POE switch (firmware 1.0.23) that had been rebooted, then left the site monitoring for recurrence.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
The duplo app needed to invert the source and destination in the alert socket message header.  The order being inverted caused some messages to not get properly routed to the nuc (if the nuc was a grs10h or rcb3) from the server.  This also caused some adjustments in the legacy client because the changed caused some connection and routing issues for the legacy devices for secondary or capture scenarios( true for both duplo nuc -> legacy monitoring or legacy nuc -> duplo monitoring).  The legacy devices now more directly associate (direct callback) received data on the alert socket to the object modeling that device.  Instead of just associating the two objects via URIs.  
Impact Assessment:  
NNC - Call Placement and Handling - Minor - Secondary and Capture connections should be a focus to make sure that connections are maintained and that alerts flow as expected.  
Platform Impact:  
grs5/grs7, rcb/rcb2/rcb3, grs10/grs10h  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  24/SEPT/2025  
Attendees - Eric Davis (Quality Engineering), Stephen Moore (Development Engineering)  
Minutes - This code change is around how alert packets are routed and affects both duplo and legacy devices. No testing around UI, VOIP, locating, dome lights or annuciation need to be included in the regression test list. In the regression meeting, we did identify some areas missing from the regression filter like reminders, service start/stop and capture/swing tests. Tests to cover these areas were added and agreed upon by both QE and Development.   
No additional software components need verification for this code change.

expected_results: Once services have fully started, no system alerts are displayed on the staff console.

description: Background: University of Miami is currently undergoing a hardware installation, where they are replacing older hardware (RCB1s and 2s, GRS5s, and GRS10s) with new hardware (RCB3s, GRS7s, GRS10Hs).  
  
Issue: On **Thursday, June 1st**, it was pointed out to on-site teams that the PBX console (which also served as the PBX NUC) was bouncing a Lost Unit Srv alert. The PBX is there to monitor for Code Calls and nothing else, making this a potential safety issue.  
This was reported to the IE behind the project, **Mark Peterson**. He proceeded to replace the GRS10, thinking it may have been something with the console. When this failed to provide the desired outcome, he set up an RCB3 to act as a NUC for the PBX to alleviate stress on the console. This also did not work. He then contacted Tech Support for assistance.

Troubleshooting/Investigation: At first, it was discovered that the GRS10’s message queue was being overloaded with messages from devices across the network. This was confirmed when I cleared the Secondary Nursing Unit list and the alerts stopped bouncing. I then proceeded to add floors back to the SNU list until the issue was recreated. The limit at the moment was five. Adding a sixth produced the bouncing alert, and adding a seventh floor put the GRS10 into a reboot cycle. These were alleviated, again, by clearing the SNU list and building it back up to five.

With the assistance of **Stephen Moore**, we were able to determine the sockets being used by the PBX were being closed. He identified that the PBX was sending out the initial handshake, which was being acknowledged by target devices. However, the sockets were being closed almost immediately thereafter.

We worked with the site’s IT team to verify the network was working as expected. DHCP and DNS are in working order, there are no firewalls in place to disrupt traffic. Nothing was discovered to that end. With the network ruled out, we turned to the hardware. We decided to split the load between two GRS10s, which cleared up the issue.

Current Situation: The PBX location for the site now has those two GRS10s installed. The site is split evenly, with six floors assigned to each. Due to the uneven number of units in the hospital (for example, 1st floor has a larger number of units to monitor compared to one of their long-term treatment floors), the GRS10 assigned to it is experiencing %CPU loads of around 50% at max. comment_summary: Rebooting a room caused Lost Unit Server alerts and high CPU on the consoles, with RCB3 boards logging huge numbers of "Invalid URI when attempting to find an entry in the route table route table". A packet capture taken on the NUC RCB3 during a room reset showed the NUC being bombarded with nboSuppressAlertsMsg messages in a repeating cycle, with the message going from the NUC to an RCB3 board and coming straight back on the same socket connection, indicating a message loop. The issue was eventually reproduced in a legacy code simulation with two nursing units, a secondary monitoring relationship and seven of ten rooms disabled, by rebooting a room from the other unit's GRS10 and restarting it, which drove the first unit's GRS10 into a very high CPU state processing the looping messages. At the customer site the problem stopped after secondary monitoring configuration was changed, and re-enabling about 20 disabled rooms on one unit also cleared it.

text: Environment: NNC and Voalte Nurse Call - All Versions

Non-Medical Device Complaints (Excel Medical, Voalte Mobile, etc.)

Explanation

---

Assign this KB to the complaint case when the following criteria are met:

- A case has been escalated to Tier 2 either for investigation or KB article evaluation, and it is determined that no technical KB article is applicable.
- Cases that have been determined as a known defect or a change request, and have a valid defect or change request ID present.
- Investigations which find a ‘one-off’ or unique error, or an error not likely to recur.
- Cases where the **Investigation Summary → Main and Sub Assembly → Reason** codes contain any of the following:
    - **3rd Party : (...)**
    - **Cancelled on customer request**
    - **Configuration Change Required/Requested** *(where the product is working as designed but the customer is requesting configuration changes)*** ** 
    - **Duplicate case**
    - **No details provided**
    - **No problem found/Could not reproduce**
    - **No response from user**
    - **User Interface/Interaction Error** *(where the product is working as designed but the end user needed to be educated on the proper use)

comment_summary: A nursing unit repeatedly raised a Lost Secondary Console call that returned after the call was cancelled and the NUC rebooted. Reviewing the basesystemsettings folder showed every secondary console in the NUC's secondary list was heartbeating except the NUC's own route id, rcb3-037221Y2WM2, which was itself present in that list; the NUC was not heartbeating with itself on either the ethernet or loopback interface, and it was the only device in the hospital with its own route id in its secondary list. The cause was identified as a monitoring criteria for a single room pointing at itself, so the NUC expected connections and heartbeats from itself and raised a Lost Secondary call when they never arrived. The fix was validated on a restored copy of the customer database before deleting the self-referencing monitoring criteria at the site and pushing configuration, after which the lost secondary call cleared with no device reboot, and no new lost secondary calls appeared for a week.

root_cause_summary: Updated configuration to resolve
investigation_details: There was a lost secondary console call that could not be cleared by any procedures to clear stuck calls - like marking the call as cancelled in the database and bouncing device service / devices.   I examined the secondary console list for the NUC that was placing the call.   This was RB 5 MB RCB3 NUC (RCB3) - 10.155.66.0 - rcb3-037221Y2WM2.  The nuc’s own ip address appeared in the list, and this was unique for the whole site - no other device had a reference to itself as a secondary.   Looking to see where the list was coming from, I found table function dbo.SecondaryConsoleConfig_GetByOrgUnitId_45.  By running the sql contained in the function, I determined that the reference to itself was coming from a monitoring criteria consisting of only a single room, many call types, and 1 org unit.    This monitoring criteria was somehow orphaned (not deleted or left behind somehow.)   After testing for safety on my machine, I deleted the monitoring criteria with sql statements, pushed configuration, and the lost secondary call disappeared.
troubleshooting_steps: Confirmed correct sw on both RCB and GRS10H. 

Confirmed no call forwarding set for the GRS10H. 

Confirmed no additional monitored units for GRS10H. 

Checked syslogs. No errors for either device. Checked configuration service log. 

Did see some other devices in the syslogs showing the invalid URI lines. 

Confirmed both effected devices are checking in successfully. 

Ran netstat on both devices. Confirmed they successfully establish to each other. 

Performed global push. No change. Purged configuration. No change. 

Forced push sw to both. No change.
troubleshooting_results: The alert makes no sense since the RCB NUC itself is not showing lost. Also the netstat proves the nuc and GRS10h are connected.
verification_summary: Determined the reference to itself was coming from a monitoring criteria consisting of only a single room, many call types, and 1 org unit. Pushed configuration, and the Lost Secondary Console alert cleared. Proper operation was confirmed & there were no patient safety issues reported. Although updating the configuration resolved issue; unable to determine how issue was caused.
rca_review_comments: Unknown how the NUC got into this state but issue has been resolved.

comment_summary: A primary GRS10 console and its NUC showed sustained high CPU utilization, with the primary console going down. Investigation found RCB3 devices continuously logging "Invalid URI when attempting to find an entry in the route table route table" in the syslog, in rooms where a GRS5 had been disabled or lost in ECT; rebooting or restarting the app on those RCB3 devices dropped NNC CPU from 65-99% back to 5-10%. The behaviour recurred at other sites with the same error signature and the same reboot remedy, but it could never be reproduced in a dev or lab environment. A later comment questions whether the FindLink log is the real problem and suggests focusing on the "Link is DOWN!!" messages and on triggering events such as a configuration push or network issue.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
The duplo app needed to invert the source and destination in the alert socket message header.  The order being inverted caused some messages to not get properly routed to the nuc (if the nuc was a grs10h or rcb3) from the server.  This also caused some adjustments in the legacy client because the changed caused some connection and routing issues for the legacy devices for secondary or capture scenarios( true for both duplo nuc -> legacy monitoring or legacy nuc -> duplo monitoring).  The legacy devices now more directly associate (direct callback) received data on the alert socket to the object modeling that device.  Instead of just associating the two objects via URIs.  
Impact Assessment:  
NNC - Call Placement and Handling - Minor - Secondary and Capture connections should be a focus to make sure that connections are maintained and that alerts flow as expected.  
Platform Impact:  
grs5/grs7, rcb/rcb2/rcb3, grs10/grs10h  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  24/SEPT/2025  
Attendees - Eric Davis (Quality Engineering), Stephen Moore (Development Engineering)  
Minutes - This code change is around how alert packets are routed and affects both duplo and legacy devices. No testing around UI, VOIP, locating, dome lights or annuciation need to be included in the regression test list. In the regression meeting, we did identify some areas missing from the regression filter like reminders, service start/stop and capture/swing tests. Tests to cover these areas were added and agreed upon by both QE and Development.   
No additional software components need verification for this code change.

* Report returned data

root_cause_summary: The 4 RCB3's that powered up fine were probably wrongly diagnosed by the installer and the failure was probably due to a bad Cat6 ethernet cable connection.  The RCB3's with the U1 and U2 failures may have failed because of a power surge on the POE Cat6 ethernet cable.  The POE switch may have been powered up when the RCB3s were  connected.  The POE switch should be powered down when connecting devices.  The Dart failure may have been a hardware failure of the module, with no root cause.
investigation_details: There were 8 RCB3's received. 4 of them power up fine and were tested on DFCT and there was no fault found. One had the C13_POE broken off the PCB, as reported by the installer.  This failure could have occurred at the manufacturer or by the installer because of rough handling.  One has a U1_POE short. Another has a U2_POE failure. The last one has a failed DART. This DART was investigated and found to be defective (Hardware failure).
verification_summary: Device replacement resolved issue.    
No corrective actions were identified; therefore, closing RCA.
rca_review_comments: The 4 RCB3's that powered up fine were probably wrongly diagnosed by the installer.  The other 4 each had a different failure.  The RCB3's with the U1 and U2 failures may have failed because of a power surge on the POE Cat6 ethernet cable.  The POE switch may have been powered up when the RCB3s were connected which can cause this type failure.  The POE switch should be powered down when connecting devices.  The Dart failure may have been a hardware failure of the module, with no root cause.  C13_POE broken off the PCB, as reported by the installer could have occurred at the manufacturer or by the installer because of rough handling.

summary: Investigate 6 returned RCB3s from Conroe Medical Center, Conroe Texas
description: Four of the 6, have damaged capacitors. C13_POE was missing on 3 of the boards and C1B was missing or damaged on 2 of the boards.  2 boards have no visible damage.  One Equipment Jack was returned where the studs that are welded to the back of the plate were broken off.
root_cause_summary: The investigation determined that the primary failure was a manufacturing process error at the contract manufacturer. Analysis of the returned RCB3 units identified one device (SN: 4618 30B WIS) that had failed Final Configuration Testing (FCT), specifically the Dome Light Speaker test, yet was still shipped to the customer. Further investigation confirmed that the device's VPD EEPROM had not been properly programmed and the manufacturer verified that the unit was released despite a failed FCT result due to operator error.

Of the six returned units, four exhibited obvious physical damage, including missing or damaged C13_POE and C1B capacitors, which prevented normal operation and suggested handling or installation-related damage. A second unit (SN: 4718 04E WIS) was fully functional during testing and no product defect could be identified.

The contract manufacturer subsequently confirmed that the failed unit was mistakenly shipped despite not passing production testing and committed to retraining the operator responsible for the test station.
investigation_details: Investigated 2 out of the 6 units (4 units were damaged and could not be powered on). No issue was detected on the RCB3 SN: 4718 04E WIS. The unit with SN: 4618 30B WIS was found to have failed the FCT.
rca_review_comments: The confirmed product failure was caused by a manufacturing quality-control breakdown in which an RCB3 that failed Final Configuration Testing was inadvertently shipped to the customer. Investigation found the device had not completed manufacturing configuration successfully and lacked proper VPD programming. The contract manufacturer verified that the release occurred due to operator error at the FCT station and implemented corrective action through operator retraining. Additional returned units exhibited physical component damage consistent with handling or installation-related causes rather than a systemic product defect.

text: Environment: NNC and Voalte Nurse Call - All Versions

Non-Medical Device Complaints (Excel Medical, Voalte Mobile, etc.)

Explanation

---

Assign this KB to the complaint case when the following criteria are met:

- A case has been escalated to Tier 2 either for investigation or KB article evaluation, and it is determined that no technical KB article is applicable.
- Cases that have been determined as a known defect or a change request, and have a valid defect or change request ID present.
- Investigations which find a ‘one-off’ or unique error, or an error not likely to recur.
- Cases where the **Investigation Summary → Main and Sub Assembly → Reason** codes contain any of the following:
    - **3rd Party : (...)**
    - **Cancelled on customer request**
    - **Configuration Change Required/Requested** *(where the product is working as designed but the customer is requesting configuration changes)*** ** 
    - **Duplicate case**
    - **No details provided**
    - **No problem found/Could not reproduce**
    - **No response from user**
    - **User Interface/Interaction Error** *(where the product is working as designed but the end user needed to be educated on the proper use)  
*

root_cause_summary: Root cause for failure --> the excessive force applied by the user of \~ 25N led to the failure.  Breakage of the lever was observed in the lab by applying an excessive force for 350 actuations.  Customer should be advised to train users to only use enough force to active a nurse call not not to force the lever beyond the stopping point.
investigation_details: The shaft of the Code lever is broken where the lever shaft enters the housing of the GRS7.  Wistron will be contacted about starting an investigation into why the levers are breaking.
verification_summary: GRS7 and GRS5 devices were subjected to force tests in the back/side/down positions to measure when the code lever fails. Results showed that a large force of over 20kg is required to break the code lever in the normal use case scenarios. They were able to simulate the breaking of the code blue lever in a similar manner to the returned devices and found that the lever is weaker when pulling to the side. This is not a normal user scenario.

Summary: No design failures were identified as it was difficult to break the code lever during normal user  
Scenario.
rca_review_comments: Excessive is the root cause here.  GRS7 code Levers has been tested at 100k cycles, with no failure and therefore if normal force is used the lever should not fail.

root_cause_summary: Broken Code Lever probably due to rough handling of the device or a fall.
investigation_details: * Code blue lever is broken.
* Other than that, the device is up and running and configurable on the ECT. All calls other than code blue work as expected.
* It is noticeable when the code lever is pulled down that it is broken, which is the main reason why the device would not ring the code blue calls.
* After opening up the device it was observed that the code blue lever is broken from the plastic support itself. Since this device is 10+ years old, the code lever can break if handled roughly.

![](blob:https://media.staging.atl-paas.net/?type=file&localId=38f512e0c4f2&id=9f3f913f-6a5d-4c53-a365-e6adb4656af1&&collection=&height=6144&occurrenceKey=null&width=8160&__contextId=null&__displayType=null&__external=false&__fileMimeType=null&__fileName=null&__fileSize=null&__mediaTraceId=null&url=null)
troubleshooting_steps: Issue: Customer reports having issues with the code blue call, when they pull the code lever it does not annunciate.  
Date/Time: 08/07/2026  
GRS10 IP Address: 10.101.97.134  
Customer troubleshooting: None.   
Additional information: They found the issue accidentally. No patient outcome reported.
verification_summary: Verification activities confirmed that the Code Blue annunciation failure was isolated to the mechanical Code Blue lever assembly on P/N: P2594NNC2C11, S/N: 0331525FWIS. Inspection revealed that the lever had broken away from its plastic support, preventing the Code Blue call from being initiated. Functional testing verified that the device remained operational, configurable through the ECT, and capable of processing all other call types as expected. The physical condition of the lever supports the identified root cause and is consistent with damage resulting from rough handling, impact, or age-related wear. The findings confirm that the reported issue was caused by a hardware failure of the Code Blue lever assembly. No additional system failures were identified, and no patient injury or adverse event was reported.
rca_review_comments: Broken Code Lever probably due to rough handling of the device or a fall.  Device is past it’s useful life.

root_cause_summary: The 4 RCB3's that powered up fine were probably wrongly diagnosed by the installer and the failure was probably due to a bad Cat6 ethernet cable connection.  The RCB3's with the U1 and U2 failures may have failed because of a power surge on the POE Cat6 ethernet cable.  The POE switch may have been powered up when the RCB3s were  connected.  The POE switch should be powered down when connecting devices.  The Dart failure may have been a hardware failure of the module, with no root cause.
investigation_details: There were 8 RCB3's received. 4 of them power up fine and were tested on DFCT and there was no fault found. One had the C13_POE broken off the PCB, as reported by the installer.  This failure could have occurred at the manufacturer or by the installer because of rough handling.  One has a U1_POE short. Another has a U2_POE failure. The last one has a failed DART. This DART was investigated and found to be defective (Hardware failure).
verification_summary: Device replacement resolved issue.    
No corrective actions were identified; therefore, closing RCA.
rca_review_comments: The 4 RCB3's that powered up fine were probably wrongly diagnosed by the installer.  The other 4 each had a different failure.  The RCB3's with the U1 and U2 failures may have failed because of a power surge on the POE Cat6 ethernet cable.  The POE switch may have been powered up when the RCB3s were connected which can cause this type failure.  The POE switch should be powered down when connecting devices.  The Dart failure may have been a hardware failure of the module, with no root cause.  C13_POE broken off the PCB, as reported by the installer could have occurred at the manufacturer or by the installer because of rough handling.

summary: Investigate 6 returned RCB3s from Conroe Medical Center, Conroe Texas
description: Four of the 6, have damaged capacitors. C13_POE was missing on 3 of the boards and C1B was missing or damaged on 2 of the boards.  2 boards have no visible damage.  One Equipment Jack was returned where the studs that are welded to the back of the plate were broken off.
root_cause_summary: The investigation determined that the primary failure was a manufacturing process error at the contract manufacturer. Analysis of the returned RCB3 units identified one device (SN: 4618 30B WIS) that had failed Final Configuration Testing (FCT), specifically the Dome Light Speaker test, yet was still shipped to the customer. Further investigation confirmed that the device's VPD EEPROM had not been properly programmed and the manufacturer verified that the unit was released despite a failed FCT result due to operator error.

Of the six returned units, four exhibited obvious physical damage, including missing or damaged C13_POE and C1B capacitors, which prevented normal operation and suggested handling or installation-related damage. A second unit (SN: 4718 04E WIS) was fully functional during testing and no product defect could be identified.

The contract manufacturer subsequently confirmed that the failed unit was mistakenly shipped despite not passing production testing and committed to retraining the operator responsible for the test station.
investigation_details: Investigated 2 out of the 6 units (4 units were damaged and could not be powered on). No issue was detected on the RCB3 SN: 4718 04E WIS. The unit with SN: 4618 30B WIS was found to have failed the FCT.
rca_review_comments: The confirmed product failure was caused by a manufacturing quality-control breakdown in which an RCB3 that failed Final Configuration Testing was inadvertently shipped to the customer. Investigation found the device had not completed manufacturing configuration successfully and lacked proper VPD programming. The contract manufacturer verified that the release occurred due to operator error at the FCT station and implemented corrective action through operator retraining. Additional returned units exhibited physical component damage consistent with handling or installation-related causes rather than a systemic product defect.

investigation_details: Case 164507:

* We found that 10 RCB’s burnt on the bottom row of POE SW3 10.253.13.8 on 3E.
* Top row is still fine.
* We worked with John Collins from their IT group and he confirmed that they have had power issues.
* We checked DHCP and MAC topology to be sure that we do not have a network issue. All functioning normally.

Case 164903:

* Remoted in and I could not ping anything on that stack of POE’s.
* Tim Cook got onsite and stated that the UPS for 3E and 3 SURG 1 units has failed in a way where it still shows that it works, but it did not deliver power to the POE’s.
* Tim moved the POE’s to the other UPS and 3E and 3 SURG 1 are back up and normal.
* Heat in the 3E closet was excessive.
* Customer has since installed a portable AC unit in this closet to bring the temp down.
* This could be related to 3E POE issue above.

Case 164930:

* Cannot ping any devices plugged into 7th floor POE stack. 7E, 7W and 7GBH are the affected units. POE's: 10.253.17.5, .6, and .7
* Craig Courtney is onsite and stated that the 7th floor closet is extremely hot and a UPS failed - much like yesterday on 3E. (above)
* Customer has installed fans in this closet.
* UPS was delivering power to two POE switches.
* The connectivity was lost to all devices because one of these switches was the network uplink to the stack. They do not have spanning tree redundancy.

All replacement parts have been sent to customer. Customer is asking for RCA on the failed RCB's and UPS's. These parts are being shipped back to Cary for RCA.

Failure of the POE caused the System Alerts and disrupted power to the RCBs attached to it. Due to poor packaging and handling 3 of the returned RCBs were damaged in shipment, I repaired one by replacing a coil, the other 2 are not repairable. I then tested the remaining 8 RCBs for power-up and serial communication, no failures. The Boot Loader, Kernel, Middleware and NNC software versions, all were acceptable.  I checked for correct EEPROM data: Mac address and serial number, no problems. When the returned POE Switch is plugged in the fans are powered but it will not power up a RCB plugged into any of the ports. Also, there is no serial communication to the POE com port. case_summary.summary: Multiple alerts, mainly bed exit and chair alarm calls, became stuck on the status board after an upgrade, even though they cleared correctly on end devices. Investigation found a race condition in the multi-threaded device service that injected duplicate call records into the RabbitMQ bus; limiting the device service to a single processing thread, along with a later device service fix, resolved the stuck calls.
case_summary.reported_issue: Multiple alerts were becoming stuck on the status board after an upgrade, while clearing normally on end devices such as GRS5, GRS7, and GRS10.
case_summary.product: Nurse Call - Status Board / Device Service
case_summary.actions_taken: Logged into the ENT server and status board and confirmed stuck bed exit calls on a unit
Restarted RabbitMQ and verified connections
Monitored call publish/remove behavior for normal and bed-disconnect calls
Restarted status board services as a temporary workaround to clear stuck calls
Set MaxNumprocessing threads to 1 for the device service
Implemented a device service fix
case_summary.resolution: Set MaxNumprecessing threads to 1 for device service
case_summary.status: resolved
case_summary.key_points: Root cause: a race condition from recent multi-threaded processing changes in the device service, injecting duplicate calls into RabbitMQ
Log evidence found showing duplicate call creation
Restarting status board services cleared the stuck calls every time prior to the fix
Issue occurred site-wide, most prevalent on North tower 4th floor

summary: Calls not clearing from Status board (intermittent)
description: VNC 4.1

After the upgrade site is experiencing intermittent stuck calls on status board, These calls are not showing on end devices, GRS5,GRS7 or GRS10’s only Status board

Most of the stuck calls are Bed exit and chair alarm calls

However I have seen a call cord disconnect be stuck, we went to the room, placed another call cord disconnect call, plugged call cord in, the newest call cleared but the old did not, which it remained on status board.

Tried multiple tests around 12:30 pm local, 3:30 est, North tower 4th floor RM 71. we placed bed exit calls, entered the room. adjusted the bed and canceled from the GRS7, alert then cleared from Status board.

While cleaning up the test room, customer turned bed exit off. Took weights off bed, zeroed the bed, call triggered and remained active in status board but not on the GRS10. Had to restart services to clear.

Restarting status board services clears the calls every time

This issue seemingly is happening across the whole site, North tower 4th floor showing the most issues.
comment_summary: Calls intermittently failed to clear from the Status board at sites running 4.1.200, severely enough that one customer paused remaining upgrade projects. Device Service Host logs for a stuck call showed the de-duplication logic failing to trigger, producing a SQL error 2601 "Cannot insert duplicate key row in object 'NCC.V_ActiveCall' with unique index 'AK_UniqueActiveCallGUID'" so call creation was abandoned, after which every subsequent status update (Answered, Cancel) failed with SQL error 257 "Implicit conversion from data type nvarchar to timestamp is not allowed" and the call never cleared. The suspicion was that a secondary or monitoring console reports the alert with the same BaseCallID but a different RequestingDeviceId, causing IsDuplicateAlertNotification() in AlertMessageHandler.cs to fail, and the affected units all used secondary consoles and unit monitoring. A separate bug was also found in the call_update stored procedure, where the row edition check compares @RowEdition to itself rather than to the stored RowEdition. The workaround that resolved it was setting MaxNumMessageProcessingThreads to 1 in the Device Service appsettings.json file, after which no further stuck-call reports were made at either site.

root_cause_summary: Recent moves to multi-threaded processing in the Device service introduced a race condition where a secondary notification from a console monitoring the location was treated as a new call rather than a duplicate.  This caused an issue where it would inject a secondary copy of the call into the RabbitMQ bus, which caused it to appear as a duplicate while the call is still active, and a stuck call when the active call is cancelled.

root_cause_summary: The root cause of this issue is unknown. The most likely cause is a race condition with the processing threads on the Mirth server that ended up freezing up the impacted customers channels. Other potential causes have been eliminated. The CPU/RAM and Memory on the Mirth server look healthy at the time of the incident and not every customer was impacted, which eliminates most issues with the Mirth VM itself. Another thought was a potential database issue, but restarting the channels resolved the issue with no further action taken to clear up database space, which makes that unlikely. If this happens again, we know what to check on the Mirth server to verify this being a processing threads race condition, but with no clear way to recreate the issue, we ultimately can't confirm the cause.
investigation_details: RabbitMQ nodes looked healthy and all up and functional, along with the federations. Next we looked to Mirth, where I found that a number of customers (six total, including the three in the RCA) were beginning to queue up. In the channels for these customers, I found that they were up and actively receiving and queueing messages, but were not processing anything new. The last processed message in any of these customers channels was about the same time (7:16am). 

To try and resolve this, I restarted the ADT channels for these customers. After they came up again, they all began processing messages again. While messages had queued up for a few hours (we resolved this issue around 9:30am), most customers had cleared and were caught up to normal again by the early afternoon.
verification_summary: Root cause inconclusive. After restarting ADT, messages started to process. Further investigation would be needed if issue were to recur.
rca_review_comments: If this happens again, we know what to check on the Mirth server to verify this being a processing threads race condition, but with no clear way to recreate the issue, we ultimately can't confirm the cause. We have monitored Mirth the past week since the incident and this has not happened again.

summary: Race Condition with Call creation from monitored units
description: https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1625   
  
When units are being monitored, the system will report multiple of the same call (GUID/BaseCallID) to the Device Service, one from the NUC of the unit where the call was generated, and N number of calls from the Consoles that are monitoring the NUC.  The system will add the call to the SQL database and then onto an in-memory list.  The system will look on the in-memory list to determine if a call that has been reported has already been raised.  Occasionally the 2nd notification of the call will come in before the injection into SQL and adding onto the in-memory list has finished occurring.  This race condition will cause the system to incorrectly identify the monitoring console’s report as a new call.  This will fail to process and eventually result in a call that is stuck in both the database and StatusBoard (RabbitMQ specifically).  
  
In the customer environment, they have a separate SQL server and other external factors that could contribute to this race condition occurring that would have to be emulated for testing.
comment_summary: The defect concerns a race condition in call creation from monitored units. Development stated the potential race condition has existed since 2012, with no explanation yet for why it only appeared with 4.1.200 and why not all 4.1.200 sites see it, and noted the same change must also be made in the cc-nc-lib-alertComponent repository. A SQL loop repeatedly selecting from dbo.call with a half second delay was used to put load on the system while attempting reproduction. The defect could not be reproduced on PDR0 and the direct test P1575-TEST-3707 passed there after being blocked in PDP28.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
Moving the default value from 2 to 1 for the MaxNumMessageProcessingThreads in the appsettings.json and code causes the service to only process 1 message at a time.  This allows the system to avoid the race condition while minimizing code changes/regression.  
Before: Failure to process a SQL Insert before a monitored NUC reports a call results in calls incorrectly being identified as a new call instead of a duplicate, throwing errors in the DeviceService log and having the calls stuck in the DB & on StatusBoard.  
After: Device Service correctly identifies the calls as duplicates.  
Impact Assessment:  
NCP - Error Handling and System Alerting - Trivial  
Platform Impact:  
N/A  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  27/OCT/2025  
Attendees - Josh Watkins (Development Engineering), Kate Papalava (Quality Engineering)  
Minutes - The call processing logic is not impacted by the change, so the direct test is sufficient for verification.  
Additional Software Components:  
N/A
steps_taken: 1\. Configure a console to monitor another unit for Normal Calls.  
2\. Set up a method to prevent the SQL call completing before the 2nd notification comes in.  
3\. Place a normal call from a monitored location.
actual_results: The system treats the 2nd notification as a new call, causing SQL errors in the Device Service log and the call is stuck in the database and in Statusboard.
expected_results: The system should detect that the 2nd notification is a duplicate and not re-process the call.
work_around: Restarting RabbitMQ service

description: Site was experiencing no updates to statusboard on either Chrome or IE. Press F5 on browser and status board would update, but continue to be stale from the point of refresh. comment_summary: Status Board periodically failed to update bed data and calls, recovering only when refreshed, at multiple sites. Bed exit calls were confirmed to reach the database with no bridge service errors, and browser observation showed messages travelling from the Service Fabric service to the web client but the client never acknowledging them, with messages stopping once SignalR reported its error; only the Service Fabric logs contained errors, not the advanced service or Windows event logs. After RabbitMQ, Service Fabric and the advanced services were restarted, bed, locating and call data again reached the web client and the database, but a remaining problem appeared in the SignalR communication between the Status Board API service and the web client, where the client fails to acknowledge messages so the connection works for about two minutes before SignalR closes or resets it. A similar occurrence was reported at another site on an earlier version, and the service cloud case was closed with the resolution recorded as restarting RabbitMQ and the bridge service and confirming calls displayed as expected.

comment_summary: The Status Board at a production site stopped updating dynamically with patient changes, active calls and staff locations, requiring a manual refresh to see any change. The Status Board log first showed the Bridge Service failing to bind port 50000, the port the Status Board uses to call back into NaviCare for patient, bed and reminder data and through which all dynamic events flow; if the port cannot be taken at deployment the bridge reports started but does not work. A scheduled server reboot did not restore dynamic updates during controlled test calls, and the logs then pointed at RabbitMQ: the RabbitMQ user configured for the Status Board service did not match the account that actually worked at the RabbitMQ management console. The Status Board microservice was redeployed with the correct credentials and, after the RabbitMQ service was stopped and restarted, the issue was resolved with no further customer reports.

case_summary.summary: A hospital reported that cancelled calls at a 1st floor ED exam room were still showing active on the status board. Investigation tied the behavior to a race condition introduced by multi-threaded processing in the device service, which caused duplicate call entries; the recorded fix was to limit the device service to a single processing thread, and follow-up monitoring showed no further stuck calls.

summary: Calls not clearing from Status board (intermittent)
description: VNC 4.1

After the upgrade site is experiencing intermittent stuck calls on status board, These calls are not showing on end devices, GRS5,GRS7 or GRS10’s only Status board

Most of the stuck calls are Bed exit and chair alarm calls

However I have seen a call cord disconnect be stuck, we went to the room, placed another call cord disconnect call, plugged call cord in, the newest call cleared but the old did not, which it remained on status board.

Tried multiple tests around 12:30 pm local, 3:30 est, North tower 4th floor RM 71. we placed bed exit calls, entered the room. adjusted the bed and canceled from the GRS7, alert then cleared from Status board.

While cleaning up the test room, customer turned bed exit off. Took weights off bed, zeroed the bed, call triggered and remained active in status board but not on the GRS10. Had to restart services to clear.

Restarting status board services clears the calls every time

This issue seemingly is happening across the whole site, North tower 4th floor showing the most issues.
comment_summary: Calls intermittently failed to clear from the Status board at sites running 4.1.200, severely enough that one customer paused remaining upgrade projects. Device Service Host logs for a stuck call showed the de-duplication logic failing to trigger, producing a SQL error 2601 "Cannot insert duplicate key row in object 'NCC.V_ActiveCall' with unique index 'AK_UniqueActiveCallGUID'" so call creation was abandoned, after which every subsequent status update (Answered, Cancel) failed with SQL error 257 "Implicit conversion from data type nvarchar to timestamp is not allowed" and the call never cleared. The suspicion was that a secondary or monitoring console reports the alert with the same BaseCallID but a different RequestingDeviceId, causing IsDuplicateAlertNotification() in AlertMessageHandler.cs to fail, and the affected units all used secondary consoles and unit monitoring. A separate bug was also found in the call_update stored procedure, where the row edition check compares @RowEdition to itself rather than to the stored RowEdition. The workaround that resolved it was setting MaxNumMessageProcessingThreads to 1 in the Device Service appsettings.json file, after which no further stuck-call reports were made at either site.

root_cause_summary: Recent moves to multi-threaded processing in the Device service introduced a race condition where a secondary notification from a console monitoring the location was treated as a new call rather than a duplicate.  This caused an issue where it would inject a secondary copy of the call into the RabbitMQ bus, which caused it to appear as a duplicate while the call is still active, and a stuck call when the active call is cancelled.

summary: Race Condition with Call creation from monitored units
description: https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-1625   
  
When units are being monitored, the system will report multiple of the same call (GUID/BaseCallID) to the Device Service, one from the NUC of the unit where the call was generated, and N number of calls from the Consoles that are monitoring the NUC.  The system will add the call to the SQL database and then onto an in-memory list.  The system will look on the in-memory list to determine if a call that has been reported has already been raised.  Occasionally the 2nd notification of the call will come in before the injection into SQL and adding onto the in-memory list has finished occurring.  This race condition will cause the system to incorrectly identify the monitoring console’s report as a new call.  This will fail to process and eventually result in a call that is stuck in both the database and StatusBoard (RabbitMQ specifically).  
  
In the customer environment, they have a separate SQL server and other external factors that could contribute to this race condition occurring that would have to be emulated for testing.
comment_summary: The defect concerns a race condition in call creation from monitored units. Development stated the potential race condition has existed since 2012, with no explanation yet for why it only appeared with 4.1.200 and why not all 4.1.200 sites see it, and noted the same change must also be made in the cc-nc-lib-alertComponent repository. A SQL loop repeatedly selecting from dbo.call with a half second delay was used to put load on the system while attempting reproduction. The defect could not be reproduced on PDR0 and the direct test P1575-TEST-3707 passed there after being blocked in PDP28.

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
Moving the default value from 2 to 1 for the MaxNumMessageProcessingThreads in the appsettings.json and code causes the service to only process 1 message at a time.  This allows the system to avoid the race condition while minimizing code changes/regression.  
Before: Failure to process a SQL Insert before a monitored NUC reports a call results in calls incorrectly being identified as a new call instead of a duplicate, throwing errors in the DeviceService log and having the calls stuck in the DB & on StatusBoard.  
After: Device Service correctly identifies the calls as duplicates.  
Impact Assessment:  
NCP - Error Handling and System Alerting - Trivial  
Platform Impact:  
N/A  
Regression Meeting:  
Date:  27/OCT/2025  
Attendees - Josh Watkins (Development Engineering), Kate Papalava (Quality Engineering)  
Minutes - The call processing logic is not impacted by the change, so the direct test is sufficient for verification.  
Additional Software Components:  
N/A
steps_taken: 1\. Configure a console to monitor another unit for Normal Calls.  
2\. Set up a method to prevent the SQL call completing before the 2nd notification comes in.  
3\. Place a normal call from a monitored location.
actual_results: The system treats the 2nd notification as a new call, causing SQL errors in the Device Service log and the call is stuck in the database and in Statusboard.
expected_results: The system should detect that the 2nd notification is a duplicate and not re-process the call.
work_around: Restarting RabbitMQ service

root_cause_summary: The root cause of this issue is unknown. The most likely cause is a race condition with the processing threads on the Mirth server that ended up freezing up the impacted customers channels. Other potential causes have been eliminated. The CPU/RAM and Memory on the Mirth server look healthy at the time of the incident and not every customer was impacted, which eliminates most issues with the Mirth VM itself. Another thought was a potential database issue, but restarting the channels resolved the issue with no further action taken to clear up database space, which makes that unlikely. If this happens again, we know what to check on the Mirth server to verify this being a processing threads race condition, but with no clear way to recreate the issue, we ultimately can't confirm the cause.
investigation_details: RabbitMQ nodes looked healthy and all up and functional, along with the federations. Next we looked to Mirth, where I found that a number of customers (six total, including the three in the RCA) were beginning to queue up. In the channels for these customers, I found that they were up and actively receiving and queueing messages, but were not processing anything new. The last processed message in any of these customers channels was about the same time (7:16am). 

To try and resolve this, I restarted the ADT channels for these customers. After they came up again, they all began processing messages again. While messages had queued up for a few hours (we resolved this issue around 9:30am), most customers had cleared and were caught up to normal again by the early afternoon.
verification_summary: Root cause inconclusive. After restarting ADT, messages started to process. Further investigation would be needed if issue were to recur.
rca_review_comments: If this happens again, we know what to check on the Mirth server to verify this being a processing threads race condition, but with no clear way to recreate the issue, we ultimately can't confirm the cause. We have monitored Mirth the past week since the incident and this has not happened again.

summary: NNC - Platform Reporting Load Script Replication Error
description: The following error is occurring on load script.

\--Load dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum  
\--Violation of UNIQUE KEY constraint 'AK_ProtocolPropertyEnum'. Cannot insert duplicate key in object 'dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum'. The duplicate key value is (0, 2).
root_cause_summary: The AK_ProtocolPropertyEnum  alternate key on the NavicareReporting.dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum table did not match the key on the NavicareEnterprise.dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum table.
investigation_details: Whys

1. Why did the Load dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum script fail?  
   Because there was a unique key constraint violation.
2. Why was there a unique key constraint violation?  
   Because the load script was attempting to insert a record with the same unique key into the dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum table.
3. Why was it necessary to alter the table dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum?  
   Because the script alters the AK_ProtocolPropertyEnum  alternate key on the NavicareReporting.dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum table to match the key on the NavicareEnterprise.dbo.ProtocolPropertyEnum table.
verification_summary: Corrected UNIQUE KEY constraint error and rebuilt SQL server replication.
rca_review_comments: This issue already been addressed in Platform Reporting 3.7. No additional actions required.

root_cause_summary: Two ADT admit messages for the same MRN reached \`PatientStaffServiceHost\` within the same millisecond on 2026-04-10 at 21:27:50.817 UTC. The MRN-uniqueness invariant is enforced only in C# (\`PatientDAL.cs:88\`/\`231\` calling \`dbo.Patient_UniqueMRN\` as a separate scalar SELECT before \`Patient_Insert_55\`), with no shared transaction and no unique index on \`dbo.Patient.MRN\` to back it up. Both threads passed the pre-check while the table was empty for that MRN and both \`Patient_Insert_55\` calls committed, producing two active rows (\`PatientID 337242\` and \`337243\`) sharing the same MRN. 

From that point forward, every subsequent ADT update or discharge attempt for the patient ran through \`PatientDAL.Update\`, which re-ran \`IsUniqueMrn\`, which now returned false because the **other** duplicate was still active — throwing \`PatientMRNNotUnique\`. The same exception fired in the discharge path (\`Inactivate → Update → IsUniqueMrn\`), where it surfaced to Voalte Admin Client as the generic "Unable to mark patient as deleted" / "Your action could not be completed" toast. The customer's ERM feed was correct; the duplicate state was created entirely on the Voalte side by a Time-Of-Check to Time-Of-Use race in our own admit pipeline. Resolved 2026-05-06 by transactional SQL cleanup that inactivated both duplicate rows after the patient physically left the facility; engineering follow-ups (filtered unique index, \`Inactivate\` skip-uniqueness) tracked separately to prevent recurrence.
investigation_details: ````
The customer reported one patient (Same MRN ) appearing in two rooms simultaneously in Voalte Admin Client at UPMC Pinnacle West Shore (NC 4.1.200): PatientID `337242` in Room 549 (LocationID `2185`) and PatientID `337243` in Room 547 (LocationID `2246`). Manual discharge from Voalte Admin Client failed with the generic toast "Your action could not be completed." HL7 ADT messages from the customer's EMR for this patient were also being silently rejected.
We pulled the customer's `AdvancedServiceLogs - UPMC Westshore.zip` archive (110 MB) and traced the failure end-to-end:
1. **Code path traced.** `PatientStaffServiceHost`'s admit pipeline (`PatientADTController.ProcessCoreADTAction` → `PatientADTService.ProcessAdmitAction` → `PatientAggregationService.CreatePatientAndAssignLocation`) validates MRN uniqueness via `PatientDAL.cs:88` (Insert) and `:231` (Update). The check calls `Patient.IsUniqueMrn` (`Patient.cs:557`) which executes a separate scalar `SELECT dbo.Patient_UniqueMRN(@MRN, @PatientId)` — independent of the subsequent `Patient_Insert_55` / `Patient_Update_55` stored proc. There is no shared transaction and no unique constraint or filtered unique index on `dbo.Patient.MRN`. The check-then-act pattern is therefore vulnerable to a Time-Of-Check to Time-Of-Use race.
2. **Race window observed in logs.** `PatientStaffServiceHost_00310.log` lines 45992–46033 (2026-04-10 21:27:50.817 UTC) shows two threads (T24 and T26) processing identical "Received transfer for Patient Id: 0 ... will be processed as an admission" messages within the same millisecond. Both reached `CreatePatientAndAssignLocation` (line 394). T26's location-assignment INSERT failed with `Patient Location Assignment failed. Table dbo.PatientLocationAssignment, Assignment already exists for LocationID 2185.` because `dbo.PatientLocationAssignment` *does* have a unique constraint on active `LocationID`. By the time that constraint fired, both threads' `Patient_Insert_55` had already committed, producing rows `337242` (T24, succeeded end-to-end and got Room 549) and `337243` (T26, orphaned — patient row stuck, location assignment rejected).
3. **Aftermath confirmed.** From 21:27:50.937 onward, every subsequent `PatientDAL.Update` (transfers, info updates, eventual A03 discharges) re-ran `IsUniqueMrn` and tripped because the *other* duplicate was still active. The exact stack shows up at `PatientStaffServiceHost_00313.log:19614` (2026-04-16 19:05:32.749 UTC) and recurs 10+ times through

root_cause_summary: The 4 RCB3's that powered up fine were probably wrongly diagnosed by the installer and the failure was probably due to a bad Cat6 ethernet cable connection.  The RCB3's with the U1 and U2 failures may have failed because of a power surge on the POE Cat6 ethernet cable.  The POE switch may have been powered up when the RCB3s were  connected.  The POE switch should be powered down when connecting devices.  The Dart failure may have been a hardware failure of the module, with no root cause.
investigation_details: There were 8 RCB3's received. 4 of them power up fine and were tested on DFCT and there was no fault found. One had the C13_POE broken off the PCB, as reported by the installer.  This failure could have occurred at the manufacturer or by the installer because of rough handling.  One has a U1_POE short. Another has a U2_POE failure. The last one has a failed DART. This DART was investigated and found to be defective (Hardware failure).
verification_summary: Device replacement resolved issue.    
No corrective actions were identified; therefore, closing RCA.
rca_review_comments: The 4 RCB3's that powered up fine were probably wrongly diagnosed by the installer.  The other 4 each had a different failure.  The RCB3's with the U1 and U2 failures may have failed because of a power surge on the POE Cat6 ethernet cable.  The POE switch may have been powered up when the RCB3s were connected which can cause this type failure.  The POE switch should be powered down when connecting devices.  The Dart failure may have been a hardware failure of the module, with no root cause.  C13_POE broken off the PCB, as reported by the installer could have occurred at the manufacturer or by the installer because of rough handling.

root_cause_summary: Only one RCB2 had a failure due to corrupt middleware.  Possible cause would be a failure of the Flash memory.  The failure of the others was probably due a problem at the customer site.
investigation_details: John Fetzner power-up and boot tested all 7 returned devices (11/16/2021): one RCB2 failed boot with a CRC error, one RCB2 had the manufacturing image and passed FCT, and the other five had 3.9.100 firmware. Steve Moore (12/21/2021) found no problems on six devices; one GAS needed touchscreen calibration and clicked with one RJ45 cable but was fine after a cable change. On iob-0241924vwis the kernel.bin differed from the release image by a few bytes, enough to fail the CRC, with no sign of an update attempt; a re-image fixes it. Lab results are attached (https://baxter-international.atlassian.net/browse/RCA-931#icft=RCA-931 returns lab test results-1.xlsx, 1/19/2022).
verification_summary: Record-review verification summary: Based on the existing Jira investigation, root-cause, review, and comment records. This summary documents previously recorded evidence; no new functional testing or independent verification was performed.

Laboratory inspection of the seven returned devices identified a CRC/kernel corruption failure on RCB2 iob-0241924vwis; a flash-memory cause was suggested but not confirmed. The other devices did not reproduce the reported failures in the documented software review, with one touchscreen/cable concern noted. Re-imaging was proposed for the corrupted device, and a replacement order was recorded. The record supports completion of the returned-device investigation, but does not establish completion of re-image validation, replacement installation or site acceptance testing. No-fault-found findings must not be represented as proof that the original site complaint was corrected. Basis: Investigation Details, Root Cause Summary and November 2021–February 2022 comments.
rca_review_comments: One true hardware/firmware failure: corrupted kernel on RCB2 iob-0241924vwis, possibly flash memory, not confirmed. No fault found on the other six; the site-side cause is speculative. Replacement devices were ordered (order 32127753, 2/10/2022).

impact_description: Impact Assessment Summary:  
We have a script which attempts to load each of the touchscreen drivers, then checks if the touchscreen for that driver is found, then unloads the driver if not found. The suspicion was that the script might not be waiting long enough before unloading the driver, so I added a "wait for settle" call which allows device events to settle for a maximum of 1 second before performing the check. The script also checks for the touchscreen using two different mechanisms (primary and secondary), and I found a problem with one of those mechanisms in certain cases so I fixed that as well.  
Impact Assessment:  
Device Platform - App - Trivial  
Platform Impact: This change impacts Nurse Call BASE Devices with touch screens

Attendees - Britten Pipher (Development Engineering), Kate Papalava (Quality Engineering)  
Minutes - The code changes only impacted GRS10H and GRS7, no legacy devices need to be verified.

investigation_details: **HW Engineering Investigation Summary**

1. The returned GRS7 device (S/N: 18250CSWM2) was tested using the Functional Circuit Test (FCT) to determine whether any hardware-related failures were present. No hardware or functional issues were identified, and the device successfully passed FCT testing. Refer to the attached FCT results for details.
2. No touchscreen hardware-related issues were found during the investigation.
3. Observation - This device utilizes an older touchscreen test methodology that verifies operation at a single point, whereas newer GRS7 revisions employ a more robust five-point touchscreen calibration and verification process.
4. Based on the investigation, the most likely cause is a race condition that results in the incorrect touchscreen driver being loaded during startup. This condition is intermittent and cannot be reproduced in a controlled manner.
5. The Software Engineering team (Rohit M.) will continue investigating potential software-related causes associated with the reported touchscreen issue.

**Conclusion:**  
No hardware failures were identified with the returned device. The touchscreen issue does not appear to be hardware-related based on the testing performed. Further investigation will be carried out by the Software Engineering team.

**SW Engineering Investigation Summary**

1. At the time of investigation, the touch controller was operational (confirmed through evtest first) and the active controller was detected as Atmel maxTouch device on I2C bus at address 0x4b. The kernel successfully registered the controller as a Linux input device.
2. The device was configured through ECT, and all functions work as expected. No bad/unresponsive touch error was found. 
3. No persistent touchscreen controller, configuration, or input-driver failure could be reproduced on the returned unit.

The hardware investigation confirmed that the touchscreen assembly was defective. When powered ON, the affected GRS7 screen would not turn ON or failed to display. A known-good touchscreen was installed in the affected GRS7 device, and the display operated as intended, indicating that the issue was isolated to the original touchscreen assembly.

* The GRS7 processor, LCD interface, and touchscreen communication paths were operating correctly.
* The failure is localized to the LED backlight circuit within the touchscreen/display assembly.

The GRS7 unit with defective screen was also tested using the FCT to verify display operation. The device successfully passed FCT Steps 17 and 18, confirming that the LCD panel retained partial functionality. However, the display failed to activate the backlight and illuminate.

summary: GRS10 Touchscreen Failed & Degraded after Pointercal File Was Replaced
description: On 02/05, 6W Staff at UVA Medical Center reported that the touchscreen functionality of the GRS10 was intermittently not working. When I evaluated the GRS10, it appeared to be functional but occasionally would have to press a button a few times to get it to register. The top-right of the screen, specifically where the Wait List icon, would not register a press, and would instead register a touch to the Rooms Disabled button directly under it. 

 

WinSCP was installed on the Enterprise server and the pointercal file was removed, and the GRS10 was rebooted. When the GRS10's calibration screen came up, the upper-right corner of the screen still gave issues with registering a press, but it did go through after a few attempts. When the GRS10 screen came up to the Calls screen, the general functionality of the screen had improved, but the upper-right part was still not working. The 6W staff opted to use Menu > Wait List to get to the Wait List as a workaround.

 

The following day on 02/06, the staff reported the screen was completely unusable. They could not identify at what point in time the screen functionality degraded. I came onsite and verified that the screen was not operable. We replaced the GRS10 and the new GRS10 is working as intended. 

 

UVA has requested this GRS10 be sent in to be evaluated by R&D to understand why the initial issues with the screen started, and why the screen degraded further after removing the pointercal file.
comment_summary: A GRS10 touchscreen failed and then degraded further after its pointercal calibration file was replaced. The original pointercal file removed from the unit was attached, and the engineer considered the upper-right corner problems most likely to stem from extended use or a hardware fault while being unsure about the remaining touchscreen behavior. A replacement GRS10 was ordered for the site and the faulty unit was returned for evaluation, which was completed with the root cause recorded in the ticket. The unit was replaced and the troubleshooting activities were captured in a knowledge base article covering inoperable touch screens on GRS10 or GRS5 devices.

summary: Primary and Secondary Consoles do not show secondary caregiver assigned to a patient
description: At Cleveland Clinic Weston, version 3.9.102, @Christopher Skotnicki reported the following:
It appears from our testing that the call details screen will only show primary caregivers.  We tested several scenarios all which failed to display the assigned secondary caregiver until they were assigned as a 2^nd^ primary caregiver.  Please see the attached document and screenshots.
The gateway service is also driving the CPU on the server (99% CPU this AM).  Stopping gateway and starting drops CPU to normal levels (30-35%) but has risen to 85%+ over 2 hours’ time.
Honorable mention - GID-1553596 - fixed in 3.9.100 - we need to check if the two are related.
root_cause_summary: Base device process staff assignments to patient as staff assignments to locations, where primary caregiver always processes changes first resulting in blank secondary caregiver details when a primary is changed to secondary in Smart Client.
investigation_details: Digging deeper into this issue - particularly the test step in the attached document where a caregiver with a secondary role is switched to the primary role - I have found the reason for this issue.   Keep in mind the following about base devices:

1) They deal only in staff to location assignments.  Staff to patient assignments are given to base devices as staff to location assignments.

2) They deal only in the fact that a staff is assigned to a location, not any other details such as primary or secondary caregiver.

**When you hit save in smart client, for each staff member, this is the order of processing:**

1) modifications to the primary roles are sent out first.

2) modifications to the secondary roles are sent out next.

3) modifications to other roles are sent next, but this is not relevant to this case.

**So when you change a staff member from primary to secondary in the same location, this happens:**

1) removal of primary assignment - base device deletes that assignment.

2) addition of secondary assignment - base device adds that assignment.

This is all good and it works.  The staff shows up on the call details screen.

**When you change a staff member from secondary to primary in the same location, this happens:**

1) addition of primary assignment - causes no change on the base side because that assignment already exists.

2) removal of secondary assignment - base device deletes the assignment.

Since the staff to location assignment no longer exists on the base side, they disappear from the call details screen.
rca_review_comments: As far as R&D can tell, this is a pre-existing issue dealing with the order of operations for staff job roles assignments on SQL lite on the GRS10 device. A defect CBL-1475  has been opened for this specific issue. Other related defects are also linked for visibility.

root_cause_summary: LDAP connections are cached in our ldap library code, and are held for a long time (maybe days.) I set up my machine to perform ldap staff synch, and it also failed in the same manner as the customer site.  Wireshark also showed no network communication at failure time.

I found root cause by adding debug logs to the code.

summary: LDAP sync connections are not disposed of after use and become stale and fail on subsequent use.
description: when the poll time is greater than, I think, 10 minutes, default is 12 hours, Novelle LDAP connections become stale and will throw an exception if re-used.  If the LDAP sync succeeds the connetions are not cleaned up.  However, if the sync fails they are.  So, the pattern is:  
1) service starts and connetion is created, sync happens, connection is left alone.  
2) 12 hours later sync is attempted again, fails, exception is thrown and the existing connections are cleaned up.  
3) 12 hours later another sync is attempted and no connections exist so new one(s) are created and the sync succeeds.  Again, connections are left alone to become stale.  
4) next sync fails like #2.  
  
Fix: after a successful sync, call Disconnect on the connections:  
DirectoryService.Disconnect();   – this is what’s called in the try/catch when the sync fails.

appsetting.json – the default poll time (LdapPollTime) is 720 (minutes) and LdapScheduledSyncTime is no longer being used 
After – 
In the same method, after a successful sync, call DirectoryServices.Disconnect() to clean up any existing connections so they will be re-created the next time an LDAP sync is performed. 
change the value for LdapPollTime to 10 (minutes) and remove LdapScheduledSyncTime from the file.

description: **Case Title:**

root_cause_summary: Inconsistent application software on 56 different devices across the facility caused malfunctions within the Smart Sync service.
investigation_details: **Why does Status Board display Server Is Offline?** The Smart Sync service facilitates the communication between Hill-Rom beds, patients, caregivers, and supports Status Board.  The service does not remain running. 

**Why does the Smart Sync service not remaining running?** The process terminates due to an unhandled exception.

 

This appeared to begin on 5/1/18 at 8:09am EST.  Initially, we thought that maybe Smart Sync was installed twice under two different user accounts.  It does not appear to be that way.  When starting Smart Sync it runs for approximately 45 seconds and then stops.  Null exceptions are occurring in the Smart Sync logs.  

We have tried uninstalling Smart Sync service and reinstalling several times, but the issue reappears.
verification_summary: RCA-338 has been reviewed by QARA.  The root cause was determined to be related to the functional design; the connection between an ioboard and SmartSync was breaking.   The ioboard was continuing to send heartbeats despite a lost connection.   SmartSync was coming back up and receiving heartbeats for devices that were not connected.   The SmartSync code would look in a dictionary for a key of what it thinks is a connected device and the key would not exist; this would throw an exception and would not be caught.  The exception would unwind all the way to the CCR core and the application would be halted by Windows.  R&D identified the need for an upgrade to fix the issue which was addressed in the 3.7 stream.  R&D confirmed that the reason it took a while for the issue to occur was because of the time needed for multiple lost connections to eventually compound to where SmartSync could no longer recover.  An improvement was identified in Story CWS13625 and addressed in 3.7.000.  This is now in a state of Done.  No other corrective actions were identified by the RCA Team at this time.  RCA-338 can move to Done.

rca_review_comments: A design limitation in the Smart Client's name resolution mechanism caused connectivity failures in multi-domain environments. description: * Nurse Call version is 4.1.100
* Client PCs have inconsistent load times when opening Admin Client tabs
* We tested two client PCs, one with 1ms latency and one with \~20ms latency

    * Client with 1ms latency loaded in 10 seconds
    * Client with 20ms latency loaded in 1.5-2 minutes

* Upon opening Admin Client's Staff tab, 3 DB queries are run per staff record, resulting in about 7500 individual queries being run each time the tab is loaded

    * This was captured via SQL profiler
    
* By comparison, a 4.0.404 system with 9999 test staff records captures the same information from the DB in about 20 queries

    * The optimizations for Smart Client were discovered and implemented after investigation of RCA-575
    * These optimizations appear to be missing in 4.1.100
    
* More detail in the attached txt document

Intermittent (appears to be latency dependent)

Ran through SQL profiler tests while client PCs connected to Admin Client.
root_cause_summary: Large number of sql statements issued when data could be retrieved with a much smaller number of statements.
investigation_details: Oliver Thompson supplied a wireshark capture which showed the large number of sql statements generated by loading the staff admin tab.  Code debugging revealed the location of defect, in the patient staff service host, file PatientStaffDAL/PatientStaffDal.Staff.cs, method GetStaffList().   A strategy is employed of 1) Get a list of staff id’s, then 2) for each id in the list, select pieces of data like nursing unit assignments, device assignments, and application roles.   This gives correct results, but generates a large number of sql statements that can take a long time to execute on a slow network link.   A more optimized strategy would be to bring back the entire contents of the tables involved with a half dozen sql statements, and perform the join ‘in memory.’     The use of the entity framework encourages this style of ‘chatty’ sql.

summary: Voalte Admin Client not loading or loading slowly on staff tab.
description: This issue was seen at Penn Presby hospital.  There are 2581 active staff members in their database.   A client with 1 millisecond latency loads the staff tab in 10 seconds, while a client with 20 millisecond latency requires 1.5 to 2 minutes to load the staff tab.
impact_description: IMPACT ASSESSMENT SUMMARY

Fixed slow loading of the Voalte Admin Client Staff tab at large / high-latency sites. The staff-list load used an N+1 (query-in-a-loop) pattern, so the number of database round-trips grew with the staff count and load time scaled with network latency (e.g. Penn Presby: \~2,581 active staff, 1.5-2 minutes to load at 20 ms latency).

Before:  
The staff-list load issued three queries per staff member (application roles, nursing-unit associations, mobile-device assignments) inside the loop, and the org-unit expand path resolved each unit with a separate per-unit lookup. Query count scaled with staff and unit count.

After:  
Each related collection is now loaded once for all staff and matched up in memory, and the nursing units are loaded once and read from an in-memory dictionary. Query count is now constant regardless of staff count. Returned data is functionally identical.

Other areas affected:  
No. Changes are confined to the Patient/Staff service read path; output is functionally identical.

IMPACT ASSESSMENT

Product Functionalities affected:

* NCP - Voalte Admin - Staff Administration  –  Minor

Read-path query optimization only: no database schema change, no API or contract change, and no change to returned data.

SUGGESTED DIRECT TESTS (verify the fix)

* Load the Staff tab against a facility seeded with a large active-staff count (e.g. 2,000+) and confirm it loads within an acceptable time.
* Repeat with added network latency (e.g. \~20 ms to the database) to mirror the reported site conditions; confirm load time no longer scales with staff count or latency.
* Confirm the staff list content is unchanged and correct - spot-check a representative sample of staff (roles, nursing-unit associations, and mobile-device assignments), or run a script to audit all staff records against the database.
* Confirm the nursing-unit (org-unit) details shown for each staff member are correct.

SUGGESTED REGRESSION TESTS (confirm nothing else broke)

* Add / edit / delete a staff member and confirm changes reflect correctly on the Staff tab.
* Staff with empty collections (no roles, no nursing unit, or no mobile device) display correctly.
* Staff assigned to multiple nursing units show all of their units.
* Small-facility sanity check (few staff) remains fast and correct.
* API interface consumers of the staff endpoint return the same data as before the change.
* Staff tab search / filter / paging behave as before.

PLATFORM IMPACT

N/A

root_cause_summary: The issue was caused by a Patient Location Assignment (PLA) record remaining active after the patient had been discharged. Investigation found that the EffectiveThru value for the patient's location assignment had been set to a future date (12/31/2021), causing the assignment to remain active in the database even though the patient was no longer active. As a result, Smart Client treated the location as occupied and prevented admission of a new patient.

Because the location assignment remained active, discharge and transfer operations did not behave correctly. SQL trace analysis showed that the normal discharge workflow was interrupted upstream and the PatientLocationAssignment_Update stored procedure was never invoked to inactivate the assignment. This left the system in an inconsistent state where the patient appeared inactive, but the room remained associated with an active location assignment.
investigation_details: See comments/summary
rca_review_comments: A stale Patient Location Assignment record remained active due to an incorrectly populated future `EffectiveThru` date. The active assignment prevented the system from releasing the room after patient discharge, causing Smart Client to treat the location as occupied and block new admissions. The issue resulted from the assignment not being properly inactivated during the discharge process, leaving patient and location status out of sync.

Unfortunately the ADT messages have been purged from 4/10 to 4/21. But the customer sent us a report of the patient journey.  
  

![](blob:https://media.staging.atl-paas.net/?type=file&localId=dad77148188b&id=68aff69a-0fff-480d-9c74-513359805a8f&&collection=&height=438&occurrenceKey=null&width=655&__contextId=null&__displayType=null&__external=false&__fileMimeType=null&__fileName=null&__fileSize=null&__mediaTraceId=null&url=null)

![](blob:https://media.staging.atl-paas.net/?type=file&localId=1e9d3b2effb5&id=7fdc743b-e6a3-4503-8d2f-40cbd8c91196&&collection=&height=1155&occurrenceKey=null&width=1679&__contextId=null&__displayType=null&__external=false&__fileMimeType=null&__fileName=null&__fileSize=null&__mediaTraceId=null&url=null)


on 4/14/2026 in the  patientstaffservicehost_00312.log states MRN is use by another patient! The patient ID being looked at is 337242. This timeframe does not correspond to any HL7 messages. The error below gets sent over and over again for patient id 337242.  

![](blob:https://media.staging.atl-paas.net/?type=file&localId=47097abbca98&id=72b6e481-8bb2-49f1-9116-d401710757d1&&collection=&height=303&occurrenceKey=null&width=1413&__contextId=null&__displayType=null&__external=false&__fileMimeType=null&__fileName=null&__fileSize=null&__mediaTraceId=null&url=null)
